# reladraw — the full documentation, for language models

Generated from the repository's agent skill and SYNTAX.md; do not edit by hand.
It describes the language on the main branch, which can run ahead of the release
on npm.

Part 1 is the guide to writing reladraw. Where it says `reference/syntax.md`, it
means Part 2, the complete syntax reference.

# Part 1 — writing reladraw


# reladraw

A text language for diagrams. Source in, standalone SVG out, no runtime dependencies.

Every other diagram language hands the arrangement to a layout engine, so where things land is an output you can't predict from what you wrote. reladraw inverts that: the file states the arrangement in the terms a person would say out loud (`right of api`, `below worker (gap: tight)`, `even with queue`), and the tool draws exactly that. It never chooses an arrangement, never moves a box to make room, and never routes a line round anything.

That matters here specifically. You can't see the SVG you produced. With auto-layout that leaves you guessing; with reladraw the arrangement is in the sentences you just wrote, and where the picture may not read as meant, the tool tells you in words.

**Show every diagram on its served page.** Whenever the user is to see a diagram, whether one you drew, one you changed, or an existing file they asked to look at, serve it with `reladraw serve`, as step 7 of the loop says. The page redraws whenever the file changes, and the user can edit and save the file from it, so you and the user work on the one file. `render --page` writes a page to send to someone else, and the bare SVG is for putting into something else, such as a README; neither is for showing.

## Check it is installed, and the same version as this skill

This skill teaches reladraw 0.29.0. Once per session, before the first render, run:

```
reladraw --version
```

- **The same:** say nothing.
- **Older, or `--version` isn't recognized** (it arrived in 0.17.1): the tool is older than this page and will refuse some of what it teaches. Tell the user, and give them `npm install -g reladraw@latest`.
- **Newer:** this skill is out of date. Tell the user, and give them `reladraw install-skill`, which asks which agents to install for and replaces it with the skill that came with their reladraw. Carry on meanwhile; where an error names a replacement spelling, trust the error over this page.

If `reladraw` isn't installed, `npx reladraw` works without installing, and `npm install -g reladraw` installs it.

## The loop

1. Write a `.reladraw` file. Where it goes depends on what it is for. A diagram that belongs to the project, one the user asked to keep or that a README or document will show, goes where they say, or beside what it describes. A diagram drawn only to show the user something, such as an explanation or a sketch of a change, goes in a folder of its own outside the project, such as `~/.cache/reladraw/` or the system's temporary folder, named after what it shows, so the project isn't littered. Tell the user where it is, so they can move it somewhere lasting if they want to keep it.
2. `reladraw check diagram.reladraw`. It prints errors and findings and writes nothing.
3. If it fails, the **error** names the line and what to write instead. Fix and re-run.
4. If it succeeds, read the **findings** it printed. Each is one line saying what may not read as meant, where, and how much:

```
diagram.reladraw:12: warning(text-overlap): text "statements" covers the top-left corner of node resolver; the overlap is 3 units wide and 2 units tall
diagram.reladraw:9: warning(edge-node-overlap): line api -> db crosses node cache, in and out of its top
```

5. Fix each finding in the source, by placing something differently or saying where a line goes, and re-run until there are none.
6. `reladraw format diagram.reladraw` before handing the file over. It lines statements up in columns and evens out spacing, by the project's `.reladraw-format` if there is one, and changes nothing about what the file draws. A file you wrote then reads like one the user's project already has.
7. Finish by showing the user the picture. Give the diagram a title with `diagram  title: "…"`, which heads the page, then run `reladraw serve diagram.reladraw` from the folder that holds the file (`cd` there first for a diagram in the outside folder of step 1), in the background, since it runs until stopped. It opens the page in the default browser: the diagram in its own colors, panning, zooming and going full screen, with an editor (Edit, or `e`) whose Save writes the file. Serve each diagram once: the page redraws by itself when you change the file, so there is nothing to tell the user to reload. Serving a second file from the same folder opens its page on the server already running and returns at once. Don't build a page of your own around it. When there is no display to open it on, as in a remote or headless session, or when the user has said not to open it, add `--no-open` and give them the address it prints. When the user wants a page to send to someone, `reladraw render diagram.reladraw --page` writes `diagram.html`, one file that needs nothing running; put it in the outside folder of step 1 with `-o` for a diagram kept in the project, so it isn't committed by mistake. Write an SVG only when something will use it, such as a README picture: `reladraw render diagram.reladraw` writes `diagram.svg` beside the source.

**The user edits the file too.** On the served page the user can change the diagram and save it, so read the file again before every change you make to it, even one you wrote a minute ago; what you remember may no longer be what is there. After each change, describe it in a few words, which the page's Versions menu shows as yours: `reladraw note diagram.reladraw "moved the cache under the API"`, run from the folder you served. With no server running it notes nothing and says so, which is fine.

A file with no errors and no findings has nothing on top of anything. That is still not the same as a good picture: re-read your source to confirm the arrangement says what you meant, and for a large diagram tell the user you have checked the findings but not seen the render.

## The one idea

**The file says where things go, and the tool draws exactly that.** A gap is the distance you wrote. A box goes where its placements put it and nothing pushes it. A line is straight between its two boxes unless you say it is square or curved or name the places it passes. Anything that overlaps is drawn overlapping and reported.

So the fix for a problem is always more said in the source, never hoping the tool will sort it out. Two boxes on one spot: place one against the other. A line through a box: say where it passes with `via:`. A text crowding a box: widen the gap.

## Writing a file

A statement starts at the beginning of a line. A long one continues onto following lines that are indented; a blank or unindented line ends it. Indentation never puts one thing inside another. `//` starts a comment and may trail a statement.

A statement is a positional head (the keyword, a name, then a text) followed by attributes and placements **in any order**. A word ending in a colon opens an attribute and nothing else does.

### Nodes

```
node <name> ["<text>" [(<text settings>)]] [<placement> | <attribute>] ...
```

Leave the text out and the node shows its name (`node parser` reads "parser"). Write `""` for a deliberately blank node. Inside a text, ` / ` (a slash with a space on each side) is a line break; `TCP/IP` and URLs survive.

The body is `shape: rectangle | document | circle | diamond | pill | parallelogram | hexagon | trapezoid | triangle | cylinder | none` (`none` is bare text, for notes and captions; a flowchart shape with no geometric name is `flow-` and its meaning, such as `flow-subprocess` or `flow-delay`; settings follow in a bracket, `shape: triangle (aim: up)`) or `icon: disk | desktop | laptop | package | cubes | cube | database`, a picture with no box. `badge: <icon>` puts a picture beside the text as part of the label. A picture outside the set is declared with `icon <name>` and SVG between `"""` marks; prefer the built-ins.

```
node dump  "nightly dump"  shape: document
node unit  icon: cube  right of dump
node drive "External HD"  badge: disk  below dump
node aside "a remark that folds" (wrap: 20)  shape: none  right of drive
```

### Placing

```
above X          below X          left of X        right of X
above-left of X  above-right of X below-left of X  below-right of X
even with X      top even with X  bottom even with X  left even with X  right even with X
```

- **Exactly one node in the file is unplaced**, the anchor. Every other is placed against something, directly or through others.
- **A gap is exact**: `none`, `tight`, `normal` (the default) or `wide`, in the placement's bracket, `right of a (gap: tight)`, or a number of the file's unit in front, `2 right of a`. A normal box is about 4 units tall.
- **A lone direction also centers on its target.** `right of a` alone puts the box level with `a`. Another placement on that axis replaces the centering: `right of a  even with b`.
- **Each axis is stated once.** Two placements on one axis are refused. The one exception: `right of a  left of b` centers the box in the space between them, and then something must say how high.
- **Several targets are one region**: `below a and b` sits under the pair, centered between them. A distance and a direction after `and` start a second placement instead: `right of a and 2 above c top` is two placements. To use a point as a target, name it first with `point p  2 above c top-center`.
- **Nothing moves a box.** Two boxes placed `right of a` both land on one spot and are reported. Chain them (`b right of a`, `c right of b`) or put them in a container with a layout.

### Containers

A dotted name is a child: `server.api` is inside `server`, and the parent is declared first. A container is the box round its children. Arrange them one of two ways:

```
node server "Server"  layout: column (widths: match)
node server.api    "API"
node server.worker "Worker"

node lab "Lab"  right of server (gap: wide)
node lab.pc   "PC"
node lab.nas  "NAS"  right of lab.pc (gap: tight)
```

`layout: column` or `layout: row` puts the children in written order; its bracket takes `gap:`, `widths: match`, and `align-children: left | center | right`. Without a layout, exactly one child is unplaced and the rest are placed against it. `shape: none` on a container draws no box, which makes a group you can place things against as one shape.

A title goes `(inside top)` by default, centered along it; `(inside top, align: left)` puts it at the top left, and `(on top)` or `(outside top)` sit it on or above the border.

### Text

Everything a text says about itself goes in brackets after it: `color`, `size` (`small | normal | large`), `wrap` (fold every n characters) and `align`.

```
style dim  text: (color: theme-muted)
node grinder "Grinder / [dim]medium-fine[/dim]"
node note "a longer remark that folds" (size: small, wrap: 30)  shape: none  below grinder (gap: tight)
```

`[dim]…[/dim]` borrows a style's text color and size for a stretch of text; a line that is all small is spaced as a small line. A style hangs the bracket off a key: `style aside  text: (size: small, color: theme-muted)`. **Always give bare text a `(wrap: n)`**, or a sentence is one long line across whatever is beside it.

### Lines

```
edge [<name>] <from> -> <to> ["<text>" [(<placement>)]] [attributes]
```

`<-`, `<->` and `--` work too, and each end may carry a mark: `a <|-- b`, `a *--o b`, `a diamond--> b`. `from:` and `to:` name the side of the first and second name written: `from: right  to: left`.

- **Straight by default**, between the two boxes and through anything in between, which is reported. `line: (path: square)` or `line: (path: curved)` for a route read off the line's own two boxes and sides.
- **`via:` lists the places a line passes**: `via: cache top` runs just above `cache`; `via: between a and b` goes through the point between them; `via: proxy` goes through a box's center. This is how to take a line round something.
- **A text sits at the middle of its line.** Place it with `(at: start)`, `(at: 1/4)`, `(above edge)`, `(on: longest level)` or `(above some_box)`. Texts never move boxes, so give a labeled line room: a `normal` gap is too short for a word, so use `(gap: 12)` or so between boxes joined by a labeled line.
- `line: (pattern: dashed, thickness: thick, corners: rounded, color: #d2904e)`; `line: red` alone is the color.

### Against a part of a box

```
node bob      "Bob the builder" (inside top)  height: 7
node bob_role "builder" (size: small)  inside bob bottom-center  shape: none
node count    "3"  on bob top-right  shape: circle
```

A box's parts are its `text`, its sides `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`, and nine points (`top-left`, `top-center`, … `center` … `bottom-right`). `inside` tucks a node within the box against that part, `outside` puts it beyond, `on` centers it on the part.

A child `inside` its own parent's corner is placed against the finished box and never grows it, so it can land on the parent's text or other children. `stays above`, `stays below`, `stays left of` or `stays right of` a sibling (or `parent text`) keeps it clear, and the box makes room: `node laptop.mark  icon: laptop  inside laptop top-right  stays above laptop.photos`. A picture beside a box's only text goes against the text instead: `1 right of drive text`.

### Styles and colors

```
style store  fill: theme-primary-subtle  border: theme-primary  badge: database
node records "Records"  style: store
```

`fill` is a box's area, `border` its outline, `line` an edge's line, and a text's color goes in its bracket. `corners: sharp` squares a box's rounded corners, and `border: (color: theme-primary, thickness: thick)` thickens its outline, the box growing to keep its padding. Prefer theme colors, which read in light and dark themes alike: `theme-primary` and `theme-secondary` are the accents, `-subtle` is an accent softened toward the page (the one to fill a box with), `theme-muted` is quieter text. A hex or CSS color stays fixed in every theme. Leave out `diagram theme:` unless the user asks for a theme; the page lets each reader pick their own.

### Links

```
node docs  "Documentation"  url: "https://example.com/docs"
edge api -> db  "SQL"  url: "https://example.com/schema"
```

**A link goes on the thing it is about, never in a text of its own.** Give the node a `url:`, or give it to a line's text when the link is about the connection. The whole box, or the line's text, becomes clickable. When asked to add links to a diagram, put `url:` on the nodes and lines already there. Don't add nodes to hold links: no column of link texts beside the diagram, and no caption with an address under each box. Add one only when the user asks to see the addresses written out.

```
// Wrong: a new text beside the thing the link belongs to
node api_link "github.com/acme/api"  shape: none  right of api

// Right: the link is on the thing itself
node api "API server"  url: "https://github.com/acme/api"
```

The address is never drawn; a reader follows it by clicking. A line with no text can carry one too, but a style can't. Quote the value, since an unquoted `//` starts a comment.

When addresses are long, or one is used on several things, declare each once with its name and badge and use it by name, so the statements stay readable. A declaration can also list several links for things that share them:

```
url orders-docs   "https://docs.example.com/orders/v2/reference" (name: "Docs")
url orders-code   "https://github.com/example/orders/tree/main/services/api" (name: "Code")
url orders-links  orders-docs  orders-code

node api "Orders API"  url: orders-links
node worker "Worker"   url: orders-docs
```

### Descriptions

```
node proxy "Proxy"  description: "Forwards each request by its path."

description for orders and to-orders """
Owns the order records. See [the docs](https://example.com/orders).
"""
```

**Notes about a thing go in its description, not in a box beside it.** A description is shown when the thing is selected on the diagram's page, and as hover text in an SVG; it is never drawn, so it can run to paragraphs and lists in Markdown. Write a short one on the statement, and a long one with `description for`, after the diagram's statements, so it doesn't crowd them. When several things share one text, name them all after `for`.

**Offer links; don't add them unasked.** When the things in a diagram have real web addresses, such as the files of a pull request on GitHub, end your reply with one line offering to link each node to its file. Never guess an address, and don't link to files on the local machine.

## A complete small file

```
// A request path, left to right.
style store  fill: theme-primary-subtle  border: theme-primary  badge: database

node browser  "Browser"
node api      "API server"  right of browser (gap: 10)
node db       "Postgres"    right of api (gap: 10)  style: store
node worker   "Worker"      below api (gap: wide)

edge browser -> api  "HTTP"
edge api -> db       "SQL"
edge worker -> db    "writes"  to: bottom  line: (path: square)

node aside "The worker shares the database / but takes no HTTP traffic." (wrap: 30)  shape: none  below worker (gap: tight)
```

## What will bite you

- **Two boxes placed the same way.** `node b right of a` and `node c right of a` put `b` and `c` on one spot. Place `c` against `b`, or use a container with `layout:`.
- **A labeled line between close boxes.** The text sits on the line and nothing widens the gap, so it covers the boxes and is reported. Give the placement a larger gap.
- **Two unplaced boxes.** Only one may be. The error names both.
- **Saying an axis twice.** `right of a  even with a` is fine; `below a  even with b` is two statements about height, and refused.
- **Old syntax.** `level with` is `even with`; `gap:` on a node goes in a placement's bracket; edge clauses like `below c` and `between a and b` are `via: c bottom` and `via: between a and b`; `contents:` is `layout: column (…)`; `at:` on a node's text is `(inside top, align: left)` and the like; `deck:` is a container, `layout: deck  cards: "Drive 1" "Drive 2"`. Each is refused with what to write instead.
- **`note`, `box` or `link`.** Not statements: a note is `node … shape: none`, and the keywords are `node` and `edge`.
- **A coordinate.** None exist. Every position is relative to something in the diagram.
- **`#` as a comment.** It opens a hex color; comments are `//`.
- **Guessing from another language.** No braces, no semicolons, no subgraphs. If you want something not written here, check `reference/syntax.md` before inventing it.

## Reference

[reference/syntax.md](reference/syntax.md) is the full syntax reference: every construct, points and regions, waypoints and named legs, bundles, sizes, guides, drawing order, the findings, what the language refuses and why, and what changed in each version. Read it when you need a construct this page doesn't cover, or when an error or a finding points at behavior you didn't expect.

# Part 2 — the syntax reference

# Syntax reference — 0.29.0

What the language accepts. The changelog at the end lists what changed in each published version; 0.17.0's changes are large, and its entry has a table of every old spelling and what to write instead.

One idea runs through all of it: **the file says where things go, and the tool draws what it says.** It never chooses an arrangement, never moves a box to make room for something, and never finds its own way round anything. Where the result may not read as meant (two boxes on one spot, a line through a box, a text on a text), it draws it as written and prints a *finding* saying where and by how much. The fix is always something you write.

The worked example is `examples/arch.reladraw`, transcribed from the hand-drawn reference beside it. Every file in `examples/` renders without findings.

## The file

### Statements and lines

A file is a list of statements. Each starts at the beginning of a line, and nothing nests. A long statement may continue onto the lines after it by indenting them:

```
node desktop1 "Desktop 1 / Linux" (inside top, align: left)
  badge: desktop
node desktop1.files "shared folder"
```

A line that starts with whitespace continues the statement above it, and a blank line or the next unindented line ends it. How much whitespace makes no difference, so nothing can depend on indentation you can't see. A bracket may stay open across lines. Indentation only lets a statement wrap; it never puts one thing inside another.

An indented line with nothing to continue, at the top of the file or after a blank line, is an error, and so is an indented line that starts with a statement keyword such as `node`. Both are almost always a stray indent, and both say to remove it.

`//` starts a comment, which runs to the end of the line and may trail a statement. An indented comment line sits inside the statement it follows; an unindented one ends it. `#` is not a comment, because it opens a hex color.

### The statements

| keyword | makes |
|---|---|
| `node` | a box, a picture, or a bare text ([Nodes](#nodes)) |
| `edge` | a line between two things ([Lines](#lines)) |
| `point` | a named point ([Points and regions](#points-and-regions)) |
| `region` | a named rectangle ([Points and regions](#points-and-regions)) |
| `bundle` | a path several lines share ([Bundles](#bundles)) |
| `guide` | a first word that makes a `node`, `edge`, `point` or `region` reference-only ([Guides](#guides)) |
| `style` | a named bundle of appearance ([Styles](#styles)) |
| `default` | appearance every thing of one kind wears ([Defaults](#defaults)) |
| `diagram` | settings for the whole drawing ([The diagram](#the-diagram)) |
| `icon` | a picture of your own ([Your own icons](#your-own-icons)) |
| `description` | text about a box or a line, for the page's panel ([Descriptions](#descriptions)) |

`box`, `link`, `note`, `deck`, `rect` and `arrow` at the start of a statement are refused by name, each quoting what to write instead.

### Heads, keys and phrases

A statement is a positional head (the keyword, a name and a text) followed by attributes and placements in any order:

```
node server "Home Server" (inside top)  left of cluster  badge: desktop
//   ^      ^             ^             ^                ^
//   name   text          its bracket   a placement      an attribute
```

What every statement of a kind has is positional; what is optional is a key. A word ending in a colon opens an attribute and nothing else does, so the two never need telling apart by position. A key may touch its value: `gap:tight` is `gap: tight`. Relations stay phrases, `right of api` or `between c and d`, because a phrase is the sentence a person would say and a key like `right-of: a` falls apart with several targets, a gap or a part.

**A value ends when its own shape is complete.** `height: 0.5 group height  right of a` reads a size, then a placement. `to: top, right of z` keeps `right of z` inside `to:`, because it is part of that value. So word order stays free and nothing is ambiguous.

**A bracket modifies the one thing it follows.** A setting that belongs to one part of a statement is written in brackets right after that part: a placement's `(gap: wide)`, a text's `(size: small, wrap: 30)`, a line's `line: (path: square)`, a layout's `layout: column (gap: none)`, a waypoint's `b top (gap: wide)`. The scope is visible instead of inferred. Inside a bracket the comma is optional, and spaces around it don't matter: `(corners: rounded,path: square)` and `(corners: rounded , path: square)` are both `(corners: rounded, path: square)`.

### Names and words

A name is unique across nodes, points, regions, lines and bundles. It may not contain `:`, which would make it a key, `,`, which separates the items of a list, or `;`, which is reserved. A dot means a child: `server.docker` is inside `server`, and the parent must be declared first. Moving a node to another parent is a rename.

Every word the language owns that has more than one part is hyphenated (`from-mark:`, `bottom-left`, `min-height:`, `align-children:`), while a phrase of separate words stays spaced (`left of`, `even with`). A name you choose should look chosen: the examples use underscores (`some_region`). `to_mark:` is refused by name, pointing to `to-mark:`.

**One spelling for each thing.** An alternative spelling is refused by name, pointing to the one the language uses: `below of a` names `below a`, and `left a` names `left of a`.

### Texts

A text is quoted. ` / `, a slash with whitespace on both sides, breaks the line, so `TCP/IP`, `16/9` and URLs survive as written. The escapes are `\"`, `\\`, `\/` (a spaced slash that doesn't break) and `\[` (a literal bracket, since `[` opens markup).

A node with no text shows its name, and a dotted name shows only its last part: `node server.docker` reads "docker". The name is never prettified. `""` says a node deliberately has none. A node drawn as a picture shows no text unless one is written.

A `"""` string takes everything between its marks as written, quotes and line breaks included. It is accepted only for an icon's SVG and a description's text ([Descriptions](#descriptions)).

### Numbers and the file's unit

A distance (a gap, a size, a padding, `2 right of a`) is measured in the file's unit, which is small: an ordinary one-line box is about 4 units tall. The gap words are whole numbers of it:

| word | units |
|---|---|
| `none` | 0 |
| `tight` | 2 |
| `normal` | 4 (the default) |
| `wide` | 8 |

A distance below the words is a number, `1 right of a` or `0.5 right of a`, and a number may start at its decimal point, `.5`. A unit is 12 pixels at the normal text size.

An appearance number is a multiple of its own normal: `(size: 1.2)` is text 20% bigger, `thickness: 2` a line twice the normal width. So a bare number has two scales, and `thickness: 1` is not `gap: 1`. The one exception is a region's `opacity:`, an amount from `0` (none) to `1.0` (solid), not a multiple of anything.

A suffix `px` fixes any of these in pixels, so it doesn't follow the file: `(size: 16px)`, `thickness: 3px`, `(gap: 12px)`. A bare number never means pixels.

A fraction is written `1/3` or as a decimal, `0.25`, and is measured from the first-named thing. **No distance is negative**: `-4 right of a` is refused, pointing to `4 left of a`, or to `inside` or `on` for a box meant to overlap.

Named values are preferred where they exist: change what `tight` means and every tight gap follows.

## Nodes

```
node <name> ["<text>" [(<text settings>)]] [<placement> | <attribute>] ...
```

### The body

Every node has one body, the thing drawn where it is, named by one of two keys.

`shape:` is the outline. A shape geometry has a word for is named by it, and takes settings in a bracket after its name for what its box doesn't decide: an amount, in the file's unit, and a direction, whose first word below is the default.

| shape | draws | its bracket |
|---|---|---|
| `rectangle` | the plain box, its corners rounded unless `corners: sharp`; the default | |
| `document` | the box with its top-right corner folded, for an artifact rather than a process; its other corners follow `corners:` | `fold:` |
| `circle` | a circle sized to hold its text; given a `width:` and a `height:` that differ, an ellipse | |
| `diamond` | a diamond, a flowchart's decision | |
| `pill` | a box with both ends round, a flowchart's start or end | |
| `parallelogram` | a slanted box, a flowchart's input or output | `slant:`, `lean: right \| left` |
| `hexagon` | a box with pointed ends, a flowchart's preparation | `point:` |
| `trapezoid` | a box narrower at one end, a flowchart's manual operation | `taper:`, `narrow: bottom \| top` |
| `triangle` | a triangle, a flowchart's merge (down) or extract (up) | `aim: down \| up \| left \| right` |
| `cylinder` | a cylinder standing, or `lying` on its side, for stored data | `cap:`, `lying` |
| `none` | no outline, fill or padding: bare text, or an invisible container | |

```
node in    "read input"  shape: parallelogram (slant: 2, lean: left)
node queue "queue"       shape: cylinder (cap: 1.5, lying)  right of in
node flat  "valid?"      shape: diamond  width: 20  height: 5  below in
```

A flowchart shape geometry has no word for is named `flow-` and what it means, and drawn the way the flowchart standard draws it, with no settings:

| shape | draws |
|---|---|
| `flow-subprocess` | a step drawn as its own chart: a box with a bar inside each side |
| `flow-document` | a document as the standard draws it, its bottom wavy |
| `flow-off-page` | continued on another page: a box pointed at the bottom |
| `flow-delay` | a delay or a wait: a box with its right end round |
| `flow-manual-input` | typed in by hand: a box whose top slopes |
| `flow-stored-data` | the standard's other storage: curved ends, the right one hollow |
| `flow-loop-start`, `flow-loop-end` | the start and end of a loop: a box with two corners cut, at the top or the bottom |
| `flow-card` | a punched card: a box with its top-left corner cut |
| `flow-display` | a screen: pointed on the left, round on the right |
| `flow-tape` | magnetic tape: a circle with a tail |
| `flow-punched-tape` | paper tape: wavy top and bottom |
| `flow-collate` | collate: two triangles point to point, its text on a patch where they meet |

`icon:` is a picture the node is drawn *as*, with no box:

| icon | means |
|---|---|
| `disk` | a physical drive |
| `desktop` | a workstation |
| `laptop` | a portable machine |
| `package` | something stored as a whole: an archive, a bucket, a sync root |
| `cubes` | several interchangeable units; always three, since it is the symbol for "several", not a count |
| `cube` | one of them |
| `database` | a store queried rather than read as files |

```
node dump "db dump / (app 1)"  shape: document
node aside "Written by a nightly cron job." (wrap: 30)  shape: none  below dump (gap: tight)
node svc  icon: cube  right of dump
```

Writing both keys is an error naming both. An unknown name is refused with the whole set, and so is a setting the shape doesn't take. A shape is named for how it looks, `diamond` and never `decision`, and no picture has two names. An icon is named for what it is: `package`, not `open-box`.

**Size and text.** A shape grows until its text, with its padding, fits at the shape's middle, the center of its area: a diamond is twice the padded text each way, and a triangle's text sits a third of the way from its base. A stated `width:` and `height:` stretch the shape to fill them, which is how a diamond is made flatter; a text that no longer fits is drawn as it is and reported as `text-overflow`. The text-position words of a [node's text](#where-it-sits), such as `(inside bottom)`, move it off the middle. `flow-collate`'s text sits on a patch of its own fill where its two triangles meet; `(fill: none)` in the text's bracket draws it without one.

**Sides.** A side of a shape is the stretch of its outline between the lines from its middle to two corners of its box: a rectangle's sides, a circle's quarters, and on a diamond the stretch round each point. So `from: right` leaves a diamond from its right point, as a flowchart's "no" does, and means the same on every shape. A corner such as `top-right` is where the line from the middle to that corner of the box meets the outline: on a circle halfway between its sides, on a diamond the middle of an edge. Several line ends on one side spread along it.

A picture can't contain anything. A `shape: none` node with children is an invisible container ([Containers](#containers)). A circle can hold other nodes, centered in it; the other shapes don't hold nodes yet, and one with children is refused.

**Corners.** `corners: sharp` draws a box's corners square, and `corners: rounded`, the default, draws them as they always were. It is the same word and values as a line's `corners:`. It reaches every outline with corners that round: a rectangle, a container, a `flow-subprocess`, and a document's three round corners, whose fold stays as it is. Every other shape is drawn with its points sharp, so `corners:` written on one is refused; from a style or a default it lands only on the nodes it can. A picture and bare text have no outline, so they refuse it too. Like a color, it never moves anything.

```
style plain  corners: sharp
node api "API"  style: plain
node spec "spec"  shape: document  corners: sharp  right of api
```

**Bare text.** `shape: none` is how to write a note, a caption or a title over a diagram. Its text starts one step smaller than a box's, because an aside at full size reads as a statement; `(size: normal)` overrides that. Nothing bounds bare text the way a border bounds a box, so give a sentence-length one a `wrap:`.

### Your own icons

`icon <name>` declares a picture, and from then on `icon: <name>` and `badge: <name>` use it as they would a built-in one. The picture is SVG, pasted between `"""` marks or read from a file:

```
icon crate """
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24">
  <path d="M3 7 L12 3 L21 7 L21 17 L12 21 L3 17 Z" fill="none" stroke="currentColor"/>
</svg>
"""

node store "Warehouse"  badge: crate
node more  icon: crate  right of store
```

- **It keeps its own colors** on every theme. What it leaves to `currentColor` takes the theme's icon color, which is how a one-color icon follows the theme.
- **It is fitted to the icon's square** by its `viewBox`, or with none by its `width` and `height`; with neither it is refused, since nothing says how big it is.
- **Its ids and class names are renamed**, so two icons that both call a gradient `a` don't collide.
- **Script is refused**: a `<script>` element or an `on…` attribute.

A letter icon is a few letters in a circle, with `letters:` and, if wanted, its colors: `icon gh  letters: "GH"  fill: #24292f  text: white`. A color left out is the theme's: the circle one of its two accents, picked from the letters so the same letters get the same one, and the letters that accent's own text color. It goes anywhere a picture does, as a node's `icon:`, a `badge:`, or a link's badge.

A file (`icon rack "./rack.svg"`) is found relative to the diagram's own file. Only the command line can read one; in the playground or a web page, paste the SVG. A declared name replaces a built-in of the same name, and declaring one name twice is an error. Every picture is drawn into the output as path data, so the SVG stays standalone.

### Badges

`badge: <icon>` makes a picture part of the node's label: the whole text, however many lines, with the picture beside it, placed as one unit.

```
node drive "External HD"  badge: disk
```

It is shorthand for a child joined to the text ([Joined to the text](#joined-to-the-text)), and this is what it stands for:

```
node drive "External HD"
node drive.badge  icon: disk  1 right of drive text  join-with: drive text
```

The text keeps its own position words, so `node d1 "Desktop 1 / Linux" (inside top, align: left)  badge: desktop` puts the label, picture and all, in the top-left corner. On a box with nothing else in it the label is centered; on a box with children it takes the title's place and the children go under it. The picture is two lines of text tall and can be named like any child (`below drive.badge`, `edge a -> drive.badge`). Declaring `drive.badge` yourself beside a `badge:` is an error naming both ways out. Only a box can wear one.

With an empty text, `node flag "" badge: disk`, the node is exactly the picture and its padding, since an empty text takes no room.

**A picture that is a thing of its own is a child**, placed like any other: `node drive.mark  icon: disk  1 right of drive text` beside the text. Placed against the text without `join-with:`, it is not part of the label: the text stays where it would be without it, and the box grows to hold both. In the corner of a box its other children size, `node laptop.mark  icon: laptop  inside laptop top-right  stays above laptop.photos` ([Against its own parent](#against-its-own-parent)). A corner of a box with nothing in it but its text is on the text.

### Padding

A stack of cards, which `deck:` used to draw, is a container: [`layout: deck`](#a-stack-of-cards-layout-deck).

`padding:` is the room between a box's edge and what it holds, in the file's unit: `padding: 2`. On a region it is measured outward instead ([Points and regions](#points-and-regions)). One side's padding is `padding-top:`, `padding-right:`, `padding-bottom:` or `padding-left:`, over `padding:` on that side only: `padding: 2  padding-right: 4` is 2 all round and 4 on the right. A container's title keeps `padding:` from the edge, so a side's padding widens the room round the children without moving the title out of its corner. A circle has no sides, so a side's padding on one is refused.

## Placing a box

A *placement* says one thing about where a node goes, and a node carries as many as it needs. Nothing else places a box: no line, no text, no neighbor.

### Directions and gaps

```
above X           below X           left of X         right of X
above-left of X   above-right of X  below-left of X   below-right of X
```

**A gap is exactly what was said.** `right of a` puts the box a `normal` gap from `a`'s right side. The gap goes in the placement's bracket, `right of a (gap: tight)`, or as a distance in front, `2 right of a`; writing both is refused as said twice. A diagonal distance is per axis: `2 below-right of a` is 2 across and 2 down.

**A lone direction also centers on its target.** `right of a` alone puts the box level with `a`'s center, because walking right from something keeps you on its center line. That half gives way as soon as another placement says how high, whichever box it is written on: with `node b right of a` and `node a even with b.1`, B goes where B.1 is level with A, rather than centered on it.

```
node parser
node resolver  right of parser
node renderer  right of resolver (gap: wide)
node notes "notes"  below resolver (gap: tight)  shape: none
```

**A gap belongs to the relationship, not the node.** One box may want different distances on different sides, so each placement carries its own. `gap:` on a node or in a style is refused, quoting the bracket form.

`right of server.docker` places a top-level node against something nested: containers scope names, not placement.

### Several targets at once

A placement may name several targets, joined by `and` or commas: `right of a, b and c`. It places against the box bounding them all, a region nobody had to declare. A distance and a direction after the `and` or comma start another placement instead: `right of a and 2 above c top` is `right of a  2 above c top`. To place against a point and a box together, name the point first: `point p  2 above c top-center`, then `right of a and p`. A lone direction centers on that region, which is how one row is offset against another:

```
node a  icon: cube
node b  right of a (gap: tight)  icon: cube
node c  right of b (gap: tight)  icon: cube
node d  below a and b (gap: tight)  icon: cube
node e  below b and c (gap: tight)  icon: cube
```

A comma promises another target, so `right of a, gap: tight` is refused, naming the comma.

### Lining up: `even with`

`even with a` shares `a`'s horizontal center line and says nothing across. A side word in front lines that side up instead: `top even with a` puts this box's top on `a`'s top. A part after the target lines up with that part: `top even with a bottom`, `top even with a center`. A side on the other axis, `top even with a left`, names no one height and is refused.

To name the axis rather than a side, put `x` or `y` in front. `x even with a` shares `a`'s vertical center line, so this box's middle across is `a`'s middle across, and says nothing about height. `y even with a` says what the bare `even with a` says: the same height.

```
node a
node b  right of a  top even with a
node c  below a (gap: wide)
node d  right of c  even with c
```

A fraction of the way across a box is written fraction first: `top even with 3/4 down a` puts this box's top three quarters of the way down `a` (`1/4 up a` says the same). Across, `left even with 1/3 across a`, counted from the left unless `from right` follows.

`even with a and b` lines up with the region round both. An alignment takes no gap, since sharing a line leaves no distance, and `(gap: …)` on one is refused.

### Part against part

`center 12 right of a center` puts the two centers exactly 12 apart, the even steps of a timeline whose boxes differ in width. `top 3 below a bottom` is the same for edges. The direction means what it always means, so with nothing else said the box also sits level with `a`'s center. A placement naming parts must give its distance: `center right of a center` is refused ("say how far").

Two distances, one per axis, are accepted in any placement: `3 below and 2 right of a`, or `top-left 3 below and 2 right of a bottom-right`. A `left` or `right` that comes first may keep its `of`: `2 right of and 3 below a` is `2 right and 3 below a`.

**How far along the side it faces.** `right of server 3/4 down` puts the box the usual gap right of `server`, its middle level with a spot three quarters of the way down `server`'s right side. `down` and `up` run along a left or right side, `across` along a top or bottom one. A word that doesn't run along the side the direction faces is refused, listing the words that do.

### Each axis is stated once

A box's position across and its position up and down each come from exactly one statement. Pinning one edge positions the box; pinning two opposite edges, `top even with a  bottom even with c`, positions and sizes it, and counts as one statement. Refused by name:

- **Said twice.** Two statements on one axis, even where they happen to agree, so a file is never right by coincidence. A bare direction beside a pin doesn't count; see below.
- **Inside out.** Two pinned edges that would give a negative size.
- **Circular.** A box measured from something measured from it.
- **An axis left open.** `right of a  left of b` with nothing up and down: centering on one or the other would decide which row the box shares, so the error names the axis.

**A direction beside a pin on its own axis gives up its distance and keeps its side.** `below trx` says two things: underneath `trx`, lined up with it across, and one gap down. A pin says how far down instead:

```
node host.bin  below host.trx  top even with cat0  bottom even with nice
```

`bin` is under `trx` across, and runs from `cat0`'s top to `nice`'s bottom. The side still has to hold: if the pins put `bin` beside or above `trx`, that is refused. A distance written on the direction, `below host.trx (gap: wide)` or `2 below host.trx`, beside a pin is refused too, since the pin would overrule it.

**Opposite placements on one axis center the box between them**, at its own size: `node c  right of a  left of b  even with a` sits in the middle of the space `a` and `b` already leave. It doesn't move `a` or `b`. If the space is too narrow, `c` overlaps them and that is reported; to make room, state how far apart `a` and `b` are.

A target need not be written first, but there must be an order in which each box can be worked out from boxes already worked out.

### One anchor

Exactly one box in the file places itself, and every other is placed relative to it, directly or through others. Two unplaced boxes are refused by name. The anchor may be split between two boxes, one saying nothing across and the other nothing up and down: with `node a "A"  even with b.1` and `node b "B" right of a`, A says nothing across, and B, once its centering on A gives way, nothing up and down. Chaining, `b right of a` then `c right of b`, is the plain way to write a few in a row; `layout:` ([Containers](#containers)) is for "these, in a line, in written order". Place against neighbors rather than hanging many boxes off one small one: a gap from a small box says nothing about the large ones also hanging off it.

### A box goes where it is placed

Nothing moves a box but its own statements. A line's text doesn't widen a gap, an arrowhead doesn't, and a line ending on a side too short for it doesn't grow the box (that is reported as `crowded-edge-ends`). **Nothing pushes overlapping boxes apart**: two boxes whose placements put them on one spot are drawn there and reported as `node-overlap`. `overlap: allow` on a node says the overlap is meant.

Identical placements don't make a list. `node b right of a` and `node c right of a` put `b` and `c` on one spot, drawn and reported. A list is a container with a layout.

### Against a part of a node

A placement's target may be a part of a node, with one of three words, each taking one part of one thing:

| | |
|---|---|
| `inside hub top-right` | wholly within, against that part |
| `outside hub right` | wholly beyond it |
| `on hub bottom-left` | centered on it, straddling it; takes no gap |

```
node bob "Bob the builder" (inside top)  height: 7
node bob_link "bob.example.com" (size: small)  inside bob bottom-center  shape: none
node mark "!"  on bob top-right  shape: circle
```

*Inside* is the direction from the part toward the box's center, so `inside right` is `left of` that side and `inside top-right` is `below-left of` that corner. `inside hub center` and `inside hub text` are refused, having no inward direction. The inset for `inside` is a gap on the placement: `tight` against another node, the parent's padding against one's own parent. Saying `inside` or `on` states the overlap, so it isn't reported.

A direction and a part stay two vocabularies: `above-left of hub` is outside it, `inside hub top-left` is a point of it, and `above hub` could never mean "the top of hub". For several boxes, name the region round them and use its part.

## Points and regions

Anywhere the language wants a position, it takes the same points: a box placed at one, a line passing through one, a line ending at one, a text placed by one.

### The parts of a box

A box's parts are its `text`, its four sides `top`, `bottom`, `left` and `right`, and its nine points:

```
top-left      top-center      top-right
left-center   center          right-center
bottom-left   bottom-center   bottom-right
```

**A side is a segment and a point is a point.** Bare `top` is the whole side; `top-center` is the one point halfway along it, which is why every midpoint carries `-center`. Naming a side leaves the other axis free. On any shape but a box, a point is where the line from the shape's middle toward that point of its box meets the outline ([Sides](#the-body)): on a circle a corner is halfway between its two sides.

A part is written as the name, then the part: `b top`, `e bottom-left`, `hub text`.

### Points

- **Between two things.** `between a and b` is the center of the space between them: halfway between their facing sides, not their centers. `between a and b at 1/3` is a third of the way across, from `a`. It always joins exactly two things with `and`; `between a, b` is refused.
- **From two things.** `down from a and left from b` is where a line straight down from `a`'s center meets a line straight left from `b`'s. A line may start from a part (`down from a left`) or a point (`left from 1 above b top-left`); from a whole side, such as `up from c top`, it starts at the side's middle. The direction words also say which way the point lies from each box, and that is checked: lines that don't meet are refused. Either half may be `even with a` instead, the level line through `a`: `up from c and even with tall top` is straight above `c`, level with `tall`'s top. It says no way the point lies, so only the other half is checked.
- **Moved by a distance.** `2 below c bottom` is 2 units below `c`'s bottom. What is moved is a point or a side, so `2 below c` is refused, asking which. A moved side is still a side: `1 above tall top` works wherever `tall top` does. A named point moves the same way: `2 above over_c`. `c bottom + 2` is refused too, since `+` adds lengths and doesn't say up or down.
- **On a line.** `req start`, `req end`, `req at 1/3` ([Points on a line](#points-on-a-line)).

A box is placed at a point with `on`, and against one with a direction:

```
node a
node b  right of a (gap: wide)  below a
node c  on down from a and left from b  shape: circle
```

`c` sits under `a` and level with `b`.

### Named points and regions

```
point funnel  between c2 and api at 2/3
region trust  web top-left to db bottom-right
region slot   between left_rack and right_rack
```

A named point can be used by several things (`via: funnel`, `below funnel`), and moving it is one edit. A named point must come out as one point, so `point p  a bottom` (a whole side) is refused.

A region is the rectangle spanned by two points, in either order. `region r  between a and b` is the space between the two boxes: on an axis where they are apart, the gap; where they overlap, only the stretch they share. `(span: both)` stretches it across both boxes on the other axis. Once named, a region has every part a box has, so `via: r center`, `right of r` and `inside r top-left` need nothing new. `padding:` pushes its edges out.

A region bounds things without owning them: they keep their own parent, aren't moved by it, and may sit in several regions, and a region may span containers. That is what separates it from a container. A point is drawn as a dot and a region as a light tint with a quiet border, unless written as a [guide](#guides). A region's fill, the tint or one it states with `fill:`, is drawn at half opacity, so overlapping regions show both colors and a region never hides what it covers; `opacity: 1.0` makes it solid, and `opacity:` takes any amount from `0` to `1.0`.

```
node web  "Web"
node api  "API"  right of web
node db   "DB"   below api
region trust  web top-left to db bottom-right  padding: 1
```

### A point's and a region's text

A point or a region may have a text, quoted after its name, with a bracket like any text's.

**A point's text sits above its dot** unless its bracket says which way: `(below)`, `(left)`, `(right)`, or a corner, `(above-right)`, `(above-left)`, `(below-right)`, `(below-left)`. There is no target, since a point's text has nothing else to sit beside. A side centers the text on the dot; a corner puts the text's nearest corner off the dot diagonally. `gap:` is the distance from the dot, half a unit unless it says.

```
node a  "A"
node b  "B"  right of a (gap: 14)
point mid "halfway" (above-right, gap: 1)  between a and b
```

**A region's text takes a container title's words**: `inside`, `on` or `outside` a side, `align:` along it, and `gap:` for its distance from the region. With nothing said it sits above the region, outside it, centered. Inside, the region makes room for it, as a container does for its title: it grows a band on that side to hold the text, and widens if the text is wider. Nothing it spans moves, but its own edges do, so whatever is placed against that side of the region moves with them. `(center)` is refused, since a region holds nothing and its middle is whatever it covers.

```
node web  "Web"
node api  "API"  right of web
node db   "DB"   below api
region trust "trust boundary" (inside top, align: left)  web top-left to db bottom-right  padding: 1
```

Both start one step smaller than a box's text, as bare text does, and take `color:`, `size:`, `wrap:`, `align:` and `reads: up` or `down`.

## Containers

A node is a container when it has children, named with a dot. **A container is the bounding box of its children, plus padding.** The children are arranged in one of two ways, never by inference.

### By hand

With no `layout:`, a container follows the file's own rule: exactly one child is unplaced, the anchor, and every other child is placed relative to it or to other children. A second unplaced child is refused, naming `layout:` as the other answer.

```
node server "Server"
node server.web "web"
node server.db  "database"  below server.web
node server.cache "cache"  right of server.db
```

A container scopes names, not placement: a child may be placed against a box outside its container, and a box outside against a child. Here `bin` is as tall as a column of boxes outside `host`:

```
node host "host"
node host.trx
node host.bin  left even with host.trx  top even with cat0  bottom even with nice
node src  left of host.trx (gap: wide)
node cat0  below src
node nice  below cat0 (gap: 6)
```

When no child is unplaced and a child is placed against a box outside, the container is placed by what it holds: it goes wherever that puts the child, and it doesn't count as a box that says nothing about where it goes.

```
node abc
node lot  below abc (gap: 4)
node host "host"
node host.trx  right of abc (gap: 6)
node host.dog  right of lot (gap: 6)
```

A container placed by its own statement can't also be placed by a child against a box outside it on the same axis. Both would say where the container goes, so it is refused as placed twice, even when the two agree; keep one of them.

### By a stated layout

`layout: column` puts every child in a column, in written order, and `layout: row` in a row. A child of a laid-out container never places itself; that is refused.

```
node svc "Ingestion and enrichment pipeline"  layout: column (widths: match)
node svc.read  "read"
node svc.parse "parse and validate"
node svc.store "store"
```

The layout's bracket takes:

| setting | says |
|---|---|
| `gap:` | the space between children; by default the same as the container's padding |
| `widths: match` | every child as wide as the widest |
| `widths: fill` | every child across the whole box; a column only |
| `align-children:` | how the children line up with each other: in a column `left`, `center` (the default) or `right`; in a row `top`, `center` or `bottom`; in a venn, the two sets, `top`, `center` or `bottom` |
| `centers: 5 apart` | space the children by their centers, not their facing sides: the even ticks of a timeline |

`centers:` beside `gap:` is refused as said twice. `layout:` on a node with no children is refused. The bare `align:` in a layout is refused, naming `align-children:` and `gather-children:`, so `align:` means one thing everywhere: where along a side.

### Two sets that overlap: `layout: venn`

A thing that belongs to two groups at once goes in the strip where they overlap. `layout: venn` takes exactly three children, in written order: the left set, the overlap, and the right set. Each keeps one parent and one dotted name, so the shared box is a child of the overlap.

```
node phases ""  layout: venn
node phases.design  "Design time"
node phases.both    ""
node phases.runtime "Runtime"

node phases.design.editor  "Editor"
node phases.both.template  "PDF template"
node phases.runtime.python "Python Lib"
```

Each set wraps its own children and the overlap's, and the two cross over the overlap. Inside each part, children are placed by hand as in any container, against their own siblings. Nothing lines boxes up across parts unless you say so: a part's anchor may be placed against a box in another part, up and down only, and its whole part moves to keep it there. `node phases.runtime.python "Python Lib"  even with phases.both.template` puts Python Lib level with the template, whatever else Runtime holds. Otherwise a shorter set is centered on the taller; `layout: venn (align-children: top)` (or `bottom`) lines the two sets up by their tops instead, as a row lines up its children. The same can be said on a set, `top even with phases.design` (or `bottom even with`) naming the other, which is the only placement a part may have; saying it both ways is refused. Either set may carry it, and either form is refused only when boxes placed across parts already decide where the sets sit. `layout: venn (heights: equal)` gives both sets the same top and bottom, each reaching as far as the other.

A set may also sit a distance lower or higher than the other: `top even with 6 below phases.design top` (or `bottom even with 2 above phases.design bottom`), the other set's same side moved, as any side can be. With `heights: equal` the two are then the same height, staggered by that much. When something inside the set is placed across parts, such as Python Lib `even with phases.both.template`, that decides where the contents go and the stagger places only the set's box, which still has to hold them; one that would cut into them is refused with how far. Across, each crossing border sits the set's padding from what is inside it and a normal gap from what is outside it; `layout: venn (gap: wide)` widens that gap, to make room for a line's text between parts.

The overlap has no border of its own. Its title follows every container's rule: drawn if it has one, nothing for `""`, and it sits centered at the top of the strip. The venn itself draws no box unless it states a fill or border. Each part gets a different fill unless it states one: the left set the theme's primary-subtle, the right its secondary-subtle, and the overlap the two laid over each other. A venn's sets crossing, and what is in the overlap sitting inside both, is never reported.

### A stack of cards: `layout: deck`

A stack of cards says "there are several of these and they are the same". `layout: deck` stacks its children, the first in front and each next one a step up and to the left behind it. When the cards are only texts, `cards:` lists them, front first:

```
node drives ""  layout: deck  cards: "Drive 1" "Drive 2" "Drive 3"
```

That is the same as writing each card as a child, which is how a card that holds anything is written, and then every card is, front first; `cards:` beside cards written out is refused, quoting them:

```
node drives ""  layout: deck
node drives.1 "Drive 1"  layout: column
node drives.1.backup "backup"
node drives.2 "Drive 2"
node drives.3 "Drive 3"
```

`cards:` names them `drives.1`, `drives.2` and on, so a line or a placement can name one card: `edge laptop -> drives.1` ends on the front card. `drives` itself is the whole stack: something placed beside, above or `even with` it measures from the stack, and a line to it ends on the stack's edge. Every card is as big as the biggest, a stated size included, and takes the front card's colors unless it states its own. A card's text sits at its top left, where it shows above the card in front, unless it says where. A card places nothing itself; the deck places it.

The deck draws nothing of its own: no outline, and nothing round its cards. A `fill:` or `border:` on it draws an outline, a padding away from the cards. Its title follows every container's rule, so it is titled with its name unless it says `""`, and it goes above the stack, centered across it, unless it says where. Cards stacked on each other are never reported as overlapping.

### Where the children sit

`gather-children:` on the box says where the group of its children sits when the box has spare room, from a stated size or a title wider than they are: against a side (`left`, `right`, `top`, `bottom`), in a corner (`top-left` and the others), or in the middle (`center`, the default). It works on any container, laid out or hand-placed; hand-placed children move as one piece.

```
node box "Services, gathered left"  gather-children: left  layout: column (align-children: right)
node box.a "a"
node box.b "a longer one"
```

That is a column with its right edges even, against the box's left side.

### A heading

A box may name one child as its heading, `heading: d1.head`, followed by the position words a title takes. The heading sits where the title would, the box makes room for it, and the other children are arranged under it. Use it for a group that is a title: an icon, a name and a version tag in a row.

```
node d1  heading: d1.head (inside top, align: left)  layout: column
node d1.head ""  shape: none  layout: row (gap: tight)
node d1.head.icon  icon: desktop
node d1.head.name  "Desktop 1" (size: normal)  shape: none
node d1.files "shared folder"
```

The heading child places nothing itself and isn't the anchor. Refused by name: a quoted text beside `heading:` (two headings), a heading that isn't a direct child, and a placement on the heading child.

### Joined to the text

`join-with: a` makes a node and `a` one unit for positioning. The node's placements still say where it sits against `a`; the join says the two move together wherever something places `a`.

```
node tall "Top"  height: 8
node tall.disk  icon: disk  1 right of tall text  top even with tall text  join-with: tall text
```

A unit that includes a box's text is placed by the text's position words: on a leaf it is centered as a pair, on a container it takes the title's place. Joins chain. In a container whose title its side words place and which has an unplaced child, a child placed only against the text, or against what is joined to it, is joined without saying so: `node d1.nw "3"  right of d1 text  even with d1 text` goes with the title. The box then holds two groups nothing relates, each fully stated; if they land on each other, that is reported as an overlap. `a` must be something one of the node's placements is against, and must be its own container's text or a sibling. A node joined to the text may be placed only against the text and what is joined to it. A box whose every child is joined to its text draws as a leaf. `badge:` is the short form.

### Against its own parent

A child placed against its parent's side or corner, `inside server right` or `inside server top-left`, is placed against the finished box and never grows it. That holds one axis at a time: `node c.j "j"  right of c.k  inside c top` is beside `c.k` across, so the box holds it across, and against the box's top down. A corner and a sibling saying the same axis, `inside c top-right  right of c.k`, are refused: the error offers `right of c.k  inside c top` and `inside c top-right  stays right of c.k` (below). If it covers something, that is reported. So is a child the box has no room for in that corner, such as a two-line picture in the corner of a box one line tall, as `node-overflow`; the box doesn't grow to fit it, since a box only just tall enough would put it level with the middle, not in the corner. To make the box hold something, place it relative to the other children, or keep it in the corner and clear of them with `stays`. Something the box holds may not be placed against a thing on its own side or corner, since the box would then depend on itself; that is refused.

**`stays` keeps a child clear of the rest of its box.** A picture in the corner of a box its children size can land on one of them. `stays above`, `stays below`, `stays left of` and `stays right of` say which way to keep clear:

```
node laptop "Laptop" (inside top, align: left)
node laptop.docs "Documents"
node laptop.photos "Photos"  right of laptop.docs
node laptop.mark  icon: laptop  inside laptop top-right  stays above laptop.photos
```

The laptop is still in the corner; `stays` never says where something goes. It says the laptop is at least the usual gap above Photos, and when it isn't, the box makes room: everything else it holds moves down together, so no gap a placement states changes, and the box grows by just enough. `(gap: wide)` or a number after the target asks for a different distance. Beside the box's own text, `stays right of drive text`, the box widens until the picture clears the text.

A limit relates two things in one box that nothing else ties together: a child placed against the box's side or corner and another child, or the box's text; two children in different corners; something beside the text and the children below it. Between two children placed against each other, or across boxes, every distance is already stated, so a limit there is refused. So is one the box can't meet by growing, such as `inside laptop bottom-right  stays above laptop.photos`, and one a stated size leaves no room for.

A title inside the border counts as content, so the box makes room for it. So does anything placed against the text. A title outside the border hangs off the box and doesn't count.

### Invisible containers

`shape: none` on a container draws no box: its edges are a tight bounding box round the children, with no padding, and anything outside can be placed against the group as one shape. Its text, if it has one, is a bare heading over the children. `node a "" shape: none` is a pure group.

```
node cluster ""  shape: none
node cluster.hub "Cloud sync"
node cluster.desktop1 "Desktop 1"  above-left of cluster.hub (gap: tight)
node cluster.laptop1  "Laptop 1"   below-left of cluster.hub (gap: tight)

node server "Home Server"  left of cluster (gap: wide)
```

`server` clears the whole cluster. Placed `left of cluster.hub`, it would only clear the hub. A [guide](#guides) node does the same and can be shown while you work.

## Sizes

A box is sized from its contents unless a size is stated, with `width:` and `height:`. A stated size is a measurement, or two pinned edges ([Each axis is stated once](#each-axis-is-stated-once)).

- **A number**, in the file's unit: `width: 30`.
- **Another box's measurement**: `height: group height`, or `height: group` for the same dimension. A box's own other dimension is the bare word: `height: 0.75 width`.
- **Scaled and added**: `height: 0.5 group height`, `height: a + b + c`, `height: group + 2`, `height: 1.25 (a + b + c)`. Multiplication before addition; parentheses only group. `*` is refused, pointing to the bare form.
- **The larger or smaller of two**: `height: larger of a and b`, `smaller of a and b`.
- **A span**: `height: a top to c bottom`.
- **Limits**, each its own key: `min-width:`, `max-width:`, `min-height:`, `max-height:`.

```
node menu "Menu"  layout: column
node menu.a "Home"
node menu.b "Settings"
node menu.c "Sign out"
node panel "Content"  right of menu  height: menu  width: 2 menu width
```

`group.height` is refused, since the dot names a child. A bracket of limits, `height: group (at most: 30)`, is refused, pointing to `max-height:`. A text that needs more room than a stated size gives is drawn as it is and reported as `text-overflow`; nothing grows a box to fit its text once its size is stated.

## A node's text

### Its bracket

Everything a text says about itself goes in brackets right after it:

```
node aside "Written nightly." (size: small, wrap: 30)  shape: none
```

| setting | takes |
|---|---|
| `color` | a color or a theme color |
| `size` | `small`, `normal` or `large`; a multiple of normal (`1.2`); or pixels (`16px`) |
| `wrap` | a count of characters to fold at, on top of ` / ` |
| `align` | how the text's own lines range: `left`, `center`, `right`, or where along a side for a title (below) |
| `fill` | on a `flow-collate` only, the patch behind its text: a color, or `none` |

`small` is 21/25 of normal and `large` the same step the other way. The names are preferred: bundled into a style, a size says *why* one text is smaller. `wrap:` is a character count, not a distance: it is how a text is made narrow and tall to sit beside something.

A style has no text of its own, so it hangs the bracket off a key: `style aside  text: (size: small, color: theme-muted)`. On a node or an edge, `text:` is refused: the bracket goes after the text.

### Where it sits

A leaf's text is centered unless its bracket says otherwise. A container's title sits against a side, said with `inside`, `on` or `outside` and the side:

| written | the title sits |
|---|---|
| `(inside top)` | along the top inside the border; the default |
| `(on top)` | on the border line, breaking it, like a form's legend |
| `(outside top)` | just above the border |
| `(center)` | in the middle of the box, as a leaf's does |

`align:` then says where along the side, and how the title's own lines range: on a top or bottom side `left`, `center` (the default) or `right`; on a left or right side `top`, `center` or `bottom`. A word that doesn't fit the side is refused, listing the three that do. The same words work on a leaf with room to spare: `node t "A tall box" (inside top)  height: 20`.

```
node hub "Hub" (inside top, align: left)  layout: row
node hub.a
node hub.b
node legend "Legend" (on top)  right of hub
node legend.a "solid: synced"  shape: none
```

**A title may be placed against the box's own children**, with any placement a child takes, the box implied: `(right even with r.d, top even with r.a)` puts the title in the top-right corner beside `r.a`, with no row of its own. A side word places the title across the side, and `align:` or a placement places it along; two words for one direction are refused. Opposite placements center the title between them, as they center a box: `(right of r.a  left of r.b, even with r.a)` sits it in the middle of the gap the two leave. A direction nothing states takes the default, `inside top` and `align: center`.

```
node r "Deployment" (right even with r.d, top even with r.a)
node r.a "north-west"
node r.d "south-east"  below-right of r.a
```

**`reads: up` and `reads: down`** turn a node's text a quarter turn, on a leaf or a title. A turned title on a left or right side takes a column one line wide rather than one word wide. The side and `align:` words still name directions on the page, so `(outside left, reads: up, align: top)` is a turned title against the upper end of the box's left side.

```
node rack "Rack 1" (inside left, reads: up)  layout: column
node rack.a "web-1"
node rack.b "web-2"
```

`at:` on a node's text is refused by name, quoting the side form, or for `at: center`, quoting `(center)` on a container and saying to write nothing on a leaf.

### Markup

A stretch of text can borrow a style's text color and size:

```
style dim  text: (color: theme-muted, size: small)
node files "shared folder / [dim]synced[/dim]"
```

The opener names a style, never a color, so the marked words borrow a meaning the file already has. A name no style answers to is refused, and so is a style that gives text neither a color nor a size.

**A line is as tall as its largest text.** A line that is all small is spaced as a small line, so the box is shorter. A small stretch mid-line, `"3 [dim]files[/dim] waiting"`, sits on the same baseline as the words around it, and the line keeps the normal spacing. With `wrap:`, a small character counts as less than a whole one, by the ratio of the two sizes. The closer repeats the name, so a mismatched close is refused by name. Marks don't nest, and a mark may cross a line break. A bare `[` is an error; write `\[` for a literal one.

## Lines

```
edge [<name>] <from> <arrow> <to> ["<text>" [(<text settings>)] ...] [<attribute>] ...
```

### The ends and their marks

```
edge a -> b       // an arrow at b
edge a <- b       // an arrow at a
edge a <-> b      // one at each end
edge a -- b       // a plain line
```

The arrow is a mark, a shaft, a mark. The shaft is `-` or `--`, and either mark may be left off. A mark is a word, or a glyph standing for one:

| mark | draws | glyph |
|---|---|---|
| `arrow` | a filled arrowhead | `>` on the right, `<` on the left |
| `oarrow` | an outlined arrowhead | `\|>` on the right, `<\|` on the left |
| `dot` | a filled circle | `*` |
| `odot` | an outlined circle | `o` |
| `diamond` | a filled diamond | |
| `odiamond` | an outlined diamond | |
| `bar` | a stroke across the line | `\|` |
| `none` | nothing | |

The `o` prefix means outlined. `o-->`, `odot--arrow`, `(odot)--(arrow)` and `[odot] -- [arrow]` are one picture. A mark must touch the shaft or be bracketed, since `edge a -- dot b` reads like a line to a node named `dot`.

`from-mark:` and `to-mark:` say the same one end at a time, which is how a style carries marks. **An end with nothing written is open, not empty**: a style may fill it, and `none` says "nothing here, whatever the style says". **A mark written in the arrow is final**: the line's own `to-mark:` may repeat it but not contradict it.

```
style inherits  to-mark: oarrow
node animal
node dog  below-left of animal
node cat  below-right of animal
edge dog -- animal  style: inherits
edge cat -- animal  style: inherits
```

**Writing order decides which end is which, never the arrow.** `a <- b` draws what `b -> a` draws, but `a` is the subject: `from:` is always the first name's end and `to:` the second's, and a text's fractions count from the first name.

**A line may be named** by a word before its ends: `edge req client -> api`. Other lines can then end on it, pass along it, or be drawn behind it.

**Each end is one name**: a box, a line, or a named point or region. `from:` and `to:` say where on it. The word before the ends, if there is one, is always the line's name, so `edge req end -> client` is a line named `req` from `end` to `client`.

```
node c
node d  right of c (gap: wide)
point a  2 below c bottom-center
point b  2 above d top-center
region pair  c top-left to d bottom-right
guide edge rail a -> b
edge c -> d  via: rail
edge pair -> a
```

**An end at a named point is exactly on it.** A point has no sides, so `from:` or `to:` on that end is refused; the line heads out toward its far end, along the axis facing it, as a side would. Several lines at one point meet there, and the arrowhead or dot sits on the point, as on another line. **An end at a region is an end at a box** the size of the region: sides, spreading and every `from:` and `to:` work as on a node.

### Where a line ends

`from:` and `to:` name a side: `edge a -> b  from: right  to: top`. The line heads straight out of that side, or straight into it. Where a side is needed and none is named, it is the side facing the other box: top and bottom for boxes sharing a stretch across, left and right for boxes sharing a stretch up and down, and for boxes placed diagonally the side the line between their centers crosses. A box and one inside it face each other with no side, so a line between them must name one.

**An end may name a point instead of a side.** `from: bottom-center` leaves from that one point, any of the nine; several ends naming one point meet there. A point along a side is written side first, then how far: `to: left 3/4 down`, `to: left 1/4 up`, `to: bottom 1/4 across`, `to: bottom 1/4 across from right`.

A square or curved line heading out of a bare corner takes whichever way gives fewer bends. To get the other, name the corner as part of a side (`from: bottom 1/1 across`), which sets the heading. Where both ways bend equally the line is refused, quoting both forms.

`from: center` aims from the box's center at the far end and starts where that aim crosses the outline, so the start slides round the box as the far end moves.

**An end may be even with another thing.** `from: right, even with cat1` is on the right side, level with `cat1`'s center; on a top or bottom side it is at `cat1`'s place across. The line heads straight out of the side, as with a bare side. The thing is anything a placement's `even with` takes: a box, a part of one (`even with cat1 top`), a fraction (`even with 3/4 down cat1`), a named point, or several (`even with a and b`, the middle of the region round them). Where that height misses the side, the end is refused, never bent. It already says where along the side, so a fraction or `, right of z` written with it is refused as saying it twice. With `straight right` it says where the line leaves from (below).

```
node bin  height: 12
node a  left of bin  top even with bin
node b  below a (gap: tight)
node engine  right of bin  even with bin  height: 12
edge a -> bin  straight right
edge b -> bin  straight right
edge bin -> engine  from: right, even with a  to: left, even with a
edge bin -> engine  from: right, even with b  to: left, even with b
```

**Several ends on one side spread evenly**, ordered by where each far box sits along the side: on a top side, the line from the leftmost box takes the leftmost slot. A line states its own place among the others with `to: top, right of z` or `from: top, right of z`, where `z` is a named line on that side; on a left or right side the words are `above` and `below`. Places stated against each other form one chain, whatever order they are written in, and a loop of them is refused. Or the box lists the whole order once, in reading order, top to bottom on a left or right side and left to right on a top or bottom one:

```
node a  right-edge-order: ae, ad, ac
edge ae a -> e  from: right
edge ad a -> d  from: right
edge ac a -> c  from: right
```

The list names every line spreading on that side, so a line left off, a name that isn't there, a line stating its own place as well, or an end pinned on that side is refused. The keys are `top-edge-order:`, `bottom-edge-order:`, `left-edge-order:` and `right-edge-order:`, written on the node itself. An end pinned to a point, or even with something, splits the side, so the others spread on either side of it.

**An end may be on another line.** `edge audit -> req` ends on the line `req`, at its middle, and `to: at 1/3` a third of the way along it. An end may also start where another line meets the same box: on a line out of `api`, `from: req end` leaves from the point where `req` ends on `api`; naming a box the line doesn't start at is refused. Lines ending on lines must be drawable in some order, so a loop of them is refused.

**A line may go from a box back to itself**, as a loop round one of its sides: `edge job -> job  from: left  to: right  via: job top  line: (path: square)` leaves the left side, runs over the top and comes back into the right side. A straight line can't loop, so a line to itself without a square or curved path is refused, quoting this form.

**A line may leave straight one way and stop at what it meets.** `edge d1 -- bus  straight down` ends where the line straight down from `d1`'s center meets `bus`. A miss is refused, never bent. This is also how a line runs level: `straight right` leaves at its own height. **`from:` may name another spot on the side it leaves from**, and the line leaves from there instead of the middle: `edge bin -> engine  from: right 1/4 down  straight right` runs level a quarter of the way down `bin`. A `from:` on any other side is refused, since the line couldn't leave it that way, and so is a `to:`, since `straight` already says where the line ends. The longer form names any box or named point or region: `to: down from z3`, or `from: left from bin` to take the height from the far end.

```
node bus "bus"  width: 40
node d1  above bus (gap: wide)
node d2  right of d1  even with d1
edge d1 -- bus  straight down
edge d2 -- bus  straight down
```

### A line is straight until told

`edge a -> c` with nothing else said is one straight segment between the two boxes, clipped at their borders, through whatever is in between. **Nothing is avoided**: a line through a box it doesn't connect is drawn over it and reported as `edge-node-overlap`. Its shape and its waypoints are how the file says otherwise, and each has one fixed meaning that never looks at the rest of the diagram.

`line: (path: straight)` is the default; `square` and `curved` are opt-in.

**A square line's route is read off its own two boxes and sides.** It has one free leg, which runs halfway between the boxes. Where both ends face the same way, it runs a step-out beyond the farther side.
