Where the ends face away from each other, each steps out and the line crosses halfway between the boxes the other way; if the boxes overlap that way there is no gap to cross, so the line runs through both and the finding names the fix, `via: a top` or `via: a bottom`. At right angles it is one corner where it can be, and otherwise goes round.

- `turn: 1/3` in the line's bracket moves the free leg a third of the way across, from the start's box. Without it, halfway.
- `step-out:` is the short first and last leg, `normal` by default: `line: (path: square, step-out: tight)`.

**A curved line follows what the file states exactly, and between two stated things it is one free sweep.** Its ends, waypoints and runs along sides are kept as written; from one to the next it is a single curve that leaves the way the line travels there and arrives the way it travels at the next. Where nothing is stated it takes the short way, over a box if one is in it, and that is reported. `curve: strong`, `normal` or `subtle` says how widely it swings. `turn:` on a curved line is a stated thing: the line passes the point where the square line's free leg would be, so the sweep becomes two.

A `turn:` that places nothing on the line it is written on is refused; from a style or `default edge` it is ignored where it can't apply.

```
node a
node b  below-right of a (gap: wide)
edge a -> b  from: right  to: left  line: (path: square)
edge a -> b  from: bottom  to: top  line: (path: curved)
```

### Waypoints

`via:` lists the places a line passes, in order:

```
node a
node b  right of a
node c  right of b
edge a -> c  from: top  to: top  via: b top
```

- **A bare part means just outside it**, a `tight` gap away. `via: b top` runs along `b`'s top from end to end, nearer end first. `via: b top (gap: wide)` sets the distance; `via: on b top` is on the border and `via: inside b top` just inside it. `via: outside b top` is refused: outside is already what `via:` means.
- **A point is one spot**: `via: b top-center`, `via: server right 3/4 down`.
- **A box's name goes through its center**: `via: proxy`.
- **Any point**: `between c and d at 1/3`, `down from a and left from b`, a named point, `req at 1/3`.
- **Through a region**: `via: through slot horizontal` runs from the region's left edge to its right. The axis is always written.
- **Alongside a named leg**: `via: above thru (gap: tight)` runs the whole length of `thru`, a tight gap above it. The side is required.

On a square line, the stretch between each pair of neighboring stops is shaped as a line between two boxes is, with one free leg; `turn:` sets all of them. A curved line sweeps from stop to stop.

**A point and a gap are different stops.** `via: between b.1 and b.2` is a point: the line goes exactly there. To cross a gap like a doorway, run through the pair's region: `region slot  between b.1 and b.2`, then `via: through slot horizontal`.

Lines through one point pinch there; they are never spread on their own. `at 1/3` and `at 2/3` part them, or a [bundle](#bundles) runs them side by side.

### Legs

Legs are named in the `via:` list: `via: leg climb, leg over_b b top, leg descent` names the three legs of a line from `a` over `b` to `c`. A `leg` entry with a place names the run along it; one without names the stretch between its neighbors. A leg's own settings go in its bracket after its name, `leg out (path: square, turn: 1/3)`, and a stop's after the stop. Legs are never counted, so adding a stop renames nothing. `leg` is required, since a bare word in `via:` is a box.

### Points on a line

A line named `req` has parts. `req start` and `req end` are where it was written to start and end. `req at 1/3` is a third of the way along it, bends included. `req b top` is `req` where it runs along `b`'s top. A named leg works anywhere a line does: `climb at 1/3`. A reference that matches two runs is refused, pointing to a `leg` name.

### Copies fan out

Copies are lines with the same two boxes on the same sides, in either direction, with nothing stated about their path. Texts and colors don't count, so a request and its response are copies. Copies are drawn as one shape, each shifted sideways from it by a fixed step like lanes on a road, so they never cross. Straight copies with no side named run parallel, a `tight` gap apart, each end landing where its lane meets the border. A line that says anything about where it goes is no longer a copy, and is drawn as written: a stated landing (`to: top, right of z`), a place in a side's `right-edge-order:` list, or a `step-out:` or `turn:` in its own bracket. That is how to override the fan. A `step-out:` or `turn:` from `default edge` or a style says the same for every line, so copies sharing it still fan, each taking it from the first.

```
node client
node api  right of client (gap: wide)
edge client -> api  "request"
edge api -> client  "response"
```

### Bundles

A bundle is a path several lines share. `bundle trunk  via: through slot horizontal` is built like a line with no ends, and a member joins with `via: trunk`, running its whole length.

```
node app1 "App 1"
node app2 "App 2"  below app1 (gap: wide)
node web "Web"  right of app1 (gap: 12)
node db "DB"  below web (gap: wide)
guide region slot  between web and db
node hub  right of slot (gap: 12)
bundle trunk  via: through slot horizontal
edge app1 -> hub  via: trunk
edge app2 -> hub  via: trunk
```

The two lines meet the gap between Web and DB, run through it side by side, and leave it together into the hub.

Its arrangement is `layout:`:

| layout | draws |
|---|---|
| `parallel` (the default) | members side by side a gap apart, `tight` unless the bracket says, so adding one widens the strip |
| `collapsed` | a bus: members merge onto the path at its start and split at its end, and the shared stretch is drawn once |
| `fan` | only on a bundle between two boxes: one curve each, widest apart at the middle |

**A parallel bundle holds one order**, so members never cross inside it. Either the bundle states it, `order: y, z, x`, listing every member by name, or members take written order and one places itself with `via: trunk (after: z)` or `(before: z)`. The two don't mix.

**A bundle may name two boxes instead of a path**: `bundle calls  a -> b  layout: fan` is the direct way between them, for copies of one line. Members must join those two boxes; `from:`, `to:` and `path:` on a member are refused, since the bundle says where its lines land.

**A bundle between two boxes can say how it gets there, as a line does**, with `from:`, `to:` and `line: (path: …)`, and `turn:` and `step-out:` in the same bracket:

```
node web "Web tier"
node ops "Ops"  below web (gap: 6)  right of web (gap: 4)
bundle logs  web -> ops  from: bottom  to: top  line: (path: square)
edge web -> ops  via: logs
edge web -> ops  via: logs
edge web -> ops  via: logs
```

The bundle's middle is routed as one line from Web's bottom to Ops's top would be. Each member runs its own lane beside it and lands where its lane meets the box, so the three leave Web side by side and arrive at Ops the same way. Where a side is too short to take the lanes at their gap, they draw closer all the way. `from:` and `to:` name a side or a point on it; `layout: fan` keeps to the direct way and is refused with any of these.

A parallel bundle's path is drawn only with guides; a collapsed one is drawn, styled with the line's own keys. A member joining or leaving partway is not built.

### A line from each child

`edge each child of a -> b` is one line from each direct child of `a` into `b`, and stays true as children are added; `a -> each child of b` likewise. Both ends is refused: pairing the children of two containers has no order to go by.

### Lines to several ends

`edge a -> b, c, d` is one line from `a` to each of `b`, `c` and `d`; `b, c and d -> a` likewise into `a`. Everything after the ends applies to every line, so `from: right-center` sends all three out of one point, to fan from there:

```
edge a -> b, c, d  from: right-center  to: left
```

Lines one statement draws share their way on purpose, so a stretch they share isn't reported as `edge-overlap`; three separate statements naming the same point are. A text is drawn once, on the line to the first name, so `"fan" (at: start)` labels the group where its lines leave together. A list on both ends is refused, for the same reason as `each child of` on both, and so is a name, which belongs to one line.

### Crossings

Where two lines cross, the later-written one is drawn on top and jumps the earlier: `crossing: gap` (the default, a short break), `arc`, `square` or `none`, on the later line. A line never jumps within reach of its own ends. Lines are drawn over boxes. [`depth:`](#drawing-order) changes either.

### The line's bracket

Everything about the line goes in its bracket, on an edge, a style or `default edge`:

```
edge web -> api  line: (color: #d2904e, path: square, corners: rounded, thickness: thick)
```

| property | takes |
|---|---|
| `color` | a color |
| `path` | `straight` (the default), `square`, `curved` |
| `corners` | `sharp` (the default), `rounded`; wherever a line has corners |
| `crossing` | `gap` (the default), `arc`, `square`, `none` |
| `pattern` | `solid` (the default), `dashed`, `dotted`, `dash-dot`; measured in thicknesses |
| `thickness` | `thin`, `normal` (the default), `thick`, a multiple of normal, or pixels (`3px`) |
| `curve` | `strong`, `normal` (the default), `subtle`; curved lines only |
| `turn` | a fraction; square and curved lines only |
| `step-out` | a distance; square and curved lines only |

`line: red` is short for `line: (color: red)`. `line: square` is refused with the bracket it meant. `corners: rounded` on a curved line is refused; from a style it lands only on lines with corners. A thick line's arrowhead grows with it, and that changes only its own drawing.

## A line's text

```
edge user -> order  "1" (at: start)  "places"  "many" (at: end)
```

A line may carry several texts, one after another, each with its own bracket. **With nothing said, a text sits at the middle of its line**, on it, with the line broken behind it. Several unplaced texts spread evenly in written order (one at the middle, three at a quarter, a half and three quarters), and placed ones cut the line into stretches: an unplaced text spreads within the stretch between the placed texts written either side of it. So write a line's texts in the order they run along it.

**Along the line:**

- `(at: 1/4)`: a fraction along the whole line, bends included, from the first name written.
- `(on: rise, at: 1/3)`: on one named leg, a fraction along it.
- `(on: longest level)`: on the line's longest piece that runs left to right, at its middle. The way to move a text off a corner. Refused on a line with no level piece.
- `(at: start)`, `(at: end)`: near an end, clear of its mark, however long the line is.

**By a box:**

- `(straight right from c)`: where a line straight right from `c`'s center first meets this line.
- `(above s1)`: just above `s1` and centered on it, as a box placed `above s1` would be, off the line if need be. A distance goes in front, as a box writes it: `(2 above s1)`. `below`, `left of` and `right of` likewise.
- `(above s1, on the line)`: stays on the line, where it first reaches that height. `gap:` sets how far above.

**Beside the line:** `(right of edge)`, `(left of edge)`, `(above edge)`, `(below edge)` move the text out the stated way until it is clear of the part of the line it landed on.

How far it moves can be said in front:

- `(at: 4/5, 1 above edge)`: one unit up from where it would sit on the line. If that is short of clear, the text still crosses the line and hides it there.
- `(at: 4/5, 1/2 clear above edge)`: half of the move that would clear the line. Any fraction or number works, `3/4 clear` or `1.5 clear`.
- `(at: 4/5, clear above edge)`: all the way clear, the same as `above edge`.

A distance is a number, `0.5 above edge`; `1/2 above edge` is refused, naming both forms. `edge-gap:` beside a distance is refused as said twice.

**Lined up with a box on one axis:** `(left even with a right)` puts the left edge of the patch behind the text at `a`'s right side, and leaves its height where it would otherwise sit; `(x even with mid1)` centers the text across on `mid1`. Any `even with` a box takes works, one per axis, and the other axis comes from the line. On a level stretch it slides the text along the line; on an upright one, it moves the text off the line sideways. With a relation that already says the same axis, such as `right of edge`, it is refused. Separate it from the bracket's next item with a comma.

**Which way it reads:** `reads: up` and `reads: down` turn it a quarter turn; `reads: along` takes the line's angle where it sits, never upside down.

`gap:` is the distance from the box for `at: start`, `at: end` and the box relations; `edge-gap:` the distance past clear for a text beside it, and part of the move that `1/2 clear` takes a fraction of. Each defaults to half a unit, written in the text's own bracket.

```
node a
node b  right of a (gap: 16)
edge a -> b  "1" (at: start)  "calls" (above edge)  "n" (at: end)
```

**The line is broken behind its text** by a patch the color of whatever is drawn under the text's middle: the page, a container's fill, or a region's tint over it. The text's bracket can say otherwise, in a box's words: `fill:` is the patch's color, `none` for no patch, and `padding:` the room it leaves round the text, all round. By default it reaches a little past the words either side and not at all above or below.

```
node a
node b  right of a (gap: 16)
edge a -> b  "beside" (above edge, fill: none)  "boxed" (at: 3/4, fill: theme-fill, padding: 0.5)
```

**A text never moves anything.** The line is drawn first and each text is measured on it. Texts that overlap are drawn and reported as `text-overlap`. A line's text takes the line's color unless its bracket says otherwise. `align:` in a line text's bracket is refused, pointing to the placement words.

## Guides

`guide` as the first word makes a `node`, `edge`, `point` or `region` reference-only:

```
node a
node b  right of a (gap: wide)
guide point funnel  between a and b
guide region slot  a top-left to b bottom-right
guide node column ""  below a  width: 10  height: 20
```

**A guide does everything its kind does except draw.** It places things, holds children, is placed against, and shapes the lines through it. A `guide node` container's children are drawn; only its box and title aren't. That gives a reserved empty space, a column to align against, or a group with no outline.

Guides are shown by whoever renders the file, not by the file: `--guides` on the command line, the Guides switch in Settings on the page and in the playground. A file that explains its own construction, such as a tutorial, may say `diagram  guides: show`. Shown guides are dashed, in the theme's secondary color, and unfilled. Their look changes per kind with `default guide node`, `default guide edge`, `default guide point` and `default guide region`; a bare `default guide` is refused, listing the four.

A container styled with no border is different: the same picture with guides hidden, but showing guides never reveals it. A guide box draws nothing, so it is left out of the overlap and overflow findings.

## Drawing order

The default order: a container before its own children, boxes before lines, an earlier line before a later one. A drawn region goes in front of every box except the ones it names, which it goes behind with everything inside them. Points are drawn last.

`depth: behind b` or `depth: in front of req` moves one thing to just behind or in front of another, and moves nothing else. A leg's name limits it to the crossings on that leg. A box moves with everything inside it. A contradiction needs a cycle, and the cycle is in the file, so it is refused naming both statements: `depth: behind a, in front of a.api`, or two things each behind the other. A style may not carry `depth:`.

## Appearance

### A color names the part it colors

| key | colors | on |
|---|---|---|
| `fill` | the inside of the outline | a box |
| `border` | the outline | a box |
| `(color: …)` after a text | the text | any node, an edge; `text: (color: …)` in a style or default |
| `line` | the line and its end marks | an edge |

A key means one thing everywhere, so it can be wrong: `border:` on a node with no outline is refused, and the error lists what that kind has. A color is written as the viewer receives it: a hex value, any CSS color, or a theme color. There is no list of color words: `green` works because it is a CSS color. A quoted color is refused, and so is a hex value without its `#`. `none` means the part isn't painted: `fill: none`.

**Changing a color never moves anything.** Size is different: a bigger text or a thicker line takes more room.

### A border's bracket

```
node host "Host"  border: (color: #d2904e, thickness: thick)
```

`border: red` is short for `border: (color: red)`. `thickness:` takes `thin`, `normal` (the default), `thick`, a multiple of normal such as `3`, or pixels such as `4px`; `border: thick` is refused with the bracket it meant. A thick border is drawn inside the box's outline and the box grows by the extra, so its padding is still measured from the inside of the stroke, a gap to its neighbor from the outside, and a line still ends on its outer edge. A stated `width:` or `height:` is the outside of the box, stroke included. A region's border is drawn inside the edge its points state, and the region doesn't grow.

### Styles

```
style backup  border: #d2904e  line: #d2904e
node mirror "shared folder / mirror"  style: backup
node nas "NAS"  right of mirror
edge mirror -> nas  style: backup
```

A style is a named bundle of appearance, worn with `style:`. Color carries meaning through the style's name rather than being written per thing. A style takes `fill`, `border`, `line`, `text`, `badge`, `icon`, `shape`, `from-mark`, `to-mark`, `padding`, `corners` and a region's `opacity`, and a title's position inside `text: (…)`: `style zone  text: (outside top, align: left)`. It never says where a thing goes, so it can't carry a placement, a `gap:`, a `depth:`, or a line's `from:` or `to:`, and it can't carry a `url:`, a `description:` or a deck's `cards:`.

- **A style may span kinds.** It gives each thing only the keys that thing has, so the style above gives nodes their border and lines their color.
- **A style must give a thing at least one key it has.** A style that dresses a thing in nothing is on the wrong thing.
- **What the statement says beats any style**, wherever `style:` sits on the line. Between styles, the later wins: `style: equipment, critical and alarm` applies in that order.
- **A key written twice on one statement is refused**, quoting both values: two words on one line are equally explicit. So is a setting twice in one bracket, `style:` twice, one style twice in a list, and a style name declared twice.

### Themes

`diagram  theme: nord` names a theme, which supplies every color the file doesn't state.

| theme | |
|---|---|
| `dark` | the default |
| `light` | the same roles on a white page |
| `solarized-dark`, `solarized-light` | [Solarized](https://ethanschoonover.com/solarized/) |
| `gruvbox-dark`, `gruvbox-light` | [Gruvbox](https://github.com/morhetz/gruvbox) |
| `catppuccin-mocha`, `catppuccin-latte` | [Catppuccin](https://catppuccin.com) |
| `nord` | [Nord](https://www.nordtheme.com) |
| `dracula` | [Dracula](https://draculatheme.com) |
| `vesper` | [Vesper](https://github.com/raunofreiberg/vesper) |
| `high-contrast-dark`, `high-contrast-light` | no fills to lean on, every line at full strength |
| `print` | a white page, black lines and no fills, for paper |

Each borrowed palette is its scheme read as a diagram (a page, a box, a border, text, a line), not a copy; their licenses are in `NOTICE`. An unknown name is refused with the list. `--theme light` on the command line overrides the file's theme, so one source renders a light and a dark image.

A theme draws a container quieter than a leaf, keyed on having children. A box whose only children are its badge, its heading or things joined to its text draws as a leaf.

### Theme colors

A color you write stays that color under every theme. To follow the theme, name a theme color. Every theme defines the same set, all beginning `theme-`:

| color | is |
|---|---|
| `theme-page` | the page |
| `theme-text` | text |
| `theme-muted` | quieter, secondary text |
| `theme-fill` | a box's fill |
| `theme-border` | a box's outline |
| `theme-line` | a line |
| `theme-primary` | the theme's signature color |
| `theme-primary-subtle` | the same, mixed toward the page |
| `theme-on-primary` | text that reads on a solid `theme-primary` |
| `theme-secondary`, `theme-secondary-subtle`, `theme-on-secondary` | the same for its second color |

```
style synced  fill: theme-primary-subtle  border: theme-primary
style live    fill: theme-primary
style dim     text: (color: theme-muted)
```

A box with a theme fill and no text color of its own gets text that reads on that fill, so `style live` needs no `text:`. A hand-picked fill gets no such help. A `theme-` name no theme defines is refused with the list.

### Defaults

```
default node       border: #4a8a5c
default leaf       fill: #2e5d3a
default container  fill: #1a2620  border: #2a3a30
default edge       line: #7a8a99  text: (color: #9aa5b1, size: small)
```

A default is a style every thing of one kind wears without naming it: `node`, `leaf` (no children but those of its label), `container` (some), `edge`, and the four `default guide` kinds. The more specific word wins, all the way down: the theme, `diagram`, `default node`, `default leaf` or `default container` or `default edge`, the thing's styles in order, and what its own line says.

A container inside another container is filled a shade further from the page than the one it sits in, so the two read as two backdrops. An invisible container (`shape: none`) doesn't count, and a stated `fill:` wins as always.

A default takes the words a style does and may wear a style of its own (`default edge  style: quiet`), laid beneath its own words. It is strict about kind, since it names its kind: `default edge  fill: red` is refused, pointing to `line:`. `icon:` is a leaf's alone. A default carries no `url:` or `description:`. Each kind is written once, and `default leaf node` is refused, naming `default leaf`.

### The diagram

```
diagram  theme: nord  background: #1e2229  text: (color: #e0e0e0)
diagram  title: "How a login reaches the database"
```

`diagram` holds what covers the whole drawing: `theme`, `background` (the page behind everything), `text: (color: …)` for every text, `guides: show`, `checks: (…)` ([Findings](#errors-and-findings)), and `title`. It has no name, since a file holds one diagram, and a second one is an error. `diagram text:` takes a color only; a text size belongs on a default.

`title:` names the drawing, in quotes. It isn't drawn: the SVG carries it as its own title, which a browser shows on the tab and a screen reader announces, and a page made with `--page` is headed with it.

### Destinations

```
node docs "Documentation"  url: "https://example.com/docs"
node store "Store"  right of docs (gap: 12)
edge docs -> store  "read first"  url: "https://example.com/order"
```

`url:` makes a thing clickable in a viewer that follows links. The whole thing is the target: a node's box and everything in it, a line and its text. The value is quoted, since an unquoted `//` starts a comment. Nothing about a destination is visible. A container's destination reaches children that name none. A line with no text may have one; an unseen wider copy of the line takes the click. A style may not carry one.

A thing can have several links, written one after another, each with a name and a badge in a bracket after it:

```
node api "Orders API"
  url: "https://docs.example.com/orders" (name: "Docs", icon: "D" (fill: #3a6ea5, text: white))
       "https://github.com/…" (name: "GitHub", icon: gh)
       "https://wiki.example.com/orders" (name: "Wiki")
```

- **`name:`** is what a reader is shown, in quotes. A link with none shows its site, such as `github.com`.
- **`icon:`** is its badge. Quoted, it is letters in a small circle, `icon: "GH"`, whose colors go in a bracket after it, `(fill: #24292f, text: white)`; left out, they are the theme's. Unquoted, it is a picture: a built-in icon, or one declared with `icon <name>` ([Your own icons](#your-own-icons)), which keeps its own colors. With no `icon:`, the badge is the first letter of the name.
- **In an SVG**, a click follows the first link, and the browser's tooltip lists them all. **On a page** made with `--page`, a click selects the thing and the panel beside the drawing lists its links; a link is followed from there ([A page for looking at a diagram](#a-page-for-looking-at-a-diagram)).

The same address twice in one `url:` is refused.

A link can be declared once, with its name and badge, and used by name. A quoted value after `url:` is an address and an unquoted one is a declared link, and the two mix in one list in the order written:

```
url orders-docs  "https://docs.example.com/orders/v2/reference" (name: "Docs", icon: "D" (fill: #3a6ea5, text: white))
url orders-code  "https://github.com/example/orders/tree/main/services/api" (name: "Code")

node api "Orders API"  url: orders-docs  orders-code
node worker "Worker"   url: orders-docs  "https://example.com/runbooks/worker" (name: "Runbook")
```

A declaration may list several links, each a quoted address or another declared name, and a use gives all of them in order:

```
url orders-links  orders-docs  orders-code  "https://wiki.example.com/orders" (name: "Wiki")

node api "Orders API"  url: orders-links
```

A declared link's name and badge are its own, so a bracket after its name in a `url:` is refused; to show it differently, declare another. A declaration may come before or after its use. Refused, each with a message: a name used but never declared, a name declared twice, a declaration that reaches itself through its own list, and a name that starts a placement, such as `below`, since a placement may follow a `url:` on the same statement.

### Descriptions

A box or a line can carry a description: text a reader asks for, shown in the panel when it is selected on a page made with `--page`, and never drawn. It can be written three ways.

On the thing's own statement, quoted:

```
node proxy "Proxy"  description: "Forwards each request by its path."
```

At a distance, for things already named, so a long text doesn't crowd the diagram's statements:

```
node proxy "Proxy"
node orders "Orders"  right of proxy
edge to-orders proxy -> orders

description for orders and to-orders """
Owns the order records.

- `/orders` lands here
- see [the docs](https://example.com/orders)
"""
```

Or named, for any box or line to take by that name:

```
description replica """
One of three identical replicas behind the proxy.
"""

node r1 "Replica 1"  description: replica
node r2 "Replica 2"  description: replica  below r1
```

`description:` takes the text quoted, or a description's name unquoted, as `icon:` takes letters quoted and a picture's name bare. `description for` names boxes and named lines, separated by commas or `and`; a name that is neither is refused. A long text goes between `"""` marks, where line breaks are kept and the indentation every line shares is taken off.

The text is Markdown, in part: paragraphs, lists (`-`, `*` or `1.`), `**bold**`, `*italic*` or `_italic_`, `` `code` `` and links, `[text](https://…)`. Anything else shows as written. A link goes to an `https:`, `http:` or `mailto:` address or a path; any other is refused.

**In an SVG**, the description is the thing's hover text, with the marks taken out and each link's address after its text. Writing one never moves anything in the drawing.

A thing has one description: two on one statement, or one there and another from `description for`, are refused. So is a name declared twice. A style and a default carry none.

## Errors and findings

An **error** means the file can't be drawn: an unknown key, two placements on one axis, a cycle. Nothing is drawn, and the message names what to write instead. A **finding** is about a picture that was drawn and may not read as meant. A render with findings succeeds.

| kind | reports | default |
|---|---|---|
| `text-overlap` | a text on another text, on a line it doesn't belong to, or on a node it doesn't belong to; a text running out past the border of the container it sits in; a node over its container's title | on |
| `text-overflow` | a text running out of a box whose stated size is too small for it | on |
| `edge-node-overlap` | a line across a node that isn't one of its ends, or through its own ends | on |
| `edge-overlap` | two lines on one run for a stretch, however short; a collapsed bundle's bus, and lines from one statement such as `edge a -> b, c`, shared on purpose, are not reported | on |
| `crowded-edge-ends` | several line ends bunched on a side too short to space them: two ends' marks would touch, or, where neither has a mark, the lines come within a third of a unit | on |
| `node-overlap` | two nodes on one spot that no layout, `inside`, `on` or `overlap: allow` accounts for; `inside hub top-right` accounts for covering `hub`, not `hub`'s other children, and a box that draws nothing (no fill, border or text) can't be covered | on |
| `node-overflow` | a node placed against its container's side or corner that the container has no room for there: less room on the far side than it keeps from the side it names | on |
| `edge-no-length` | a line between two boxes that touch, drawn as its marks at the seam | on |
| `edge-crossings` | two lines crossing | off |

A finding is one line, in the form editors already read:

```
diagram.reladraw:12: warning(text-overlap): text "statements" covers the top-left corner of node resolver; the overlap is 3 units wide and 2 units tall
```

The file and line of the statement at fault, `warning` in a fixed spot, the kind, then what happened, saying where and how much in the file's unit, so the fix is plain without the picture. A finding never chooses a fix, though it may list the ways to write one.

Kinds are turned on or off by name, in the file or on the command line: `diagram  checks: (edge-crossings: on, crowded-edge-ends: off)`, or `--checks "edge-crossings: on"`. A kind not mentioned keeps its default. A deliberate overlap is stated on the thing itself (`overlap: allow`), not turned off for the whole file.

On a page written by `render --page`, the findings are listed in the side panel. On a page that edits, the playground and `serve`'s page, nothing is checked until **Check** (or `c`) is pressed, unless **Check as I type** is on in the Settings menu; an edit after a check dims the findings rather than clearing them. While the source is shown, they appear in a band under the picture, the first three of them, with **View all** to open the side panel; × closes the band until the next check. An error that stops the diagram drawing heads the list in the side panel. Clicking a finding lights what its statement drew, and, with the source shown, selects its line.

## The command line

```
reladraw render diagram.reladraw -o diagram.svg
reladraw check diagram.reladraw
```

`render` draws the SVG and prints any findings. `check` does the same layout and prints only the findings, writing nothing, so an agent iterating leaves a good SVG alone. The bare `reladraw diagram.reladraw` is refused, pointing to `reladraw render`, and a mistyped command is reported with the near match.

| option | |
|---|---|
| `-o`, `--out` | where `render` writes; defaults to the input with `.svg`; `-` for standard output |
| `--page` | `render` writes a page for looking at the diagram instead, defaulting to the input with `.html` |
| `--theme <name>` | render in another theme, whatever the file says |
| `--guides` | draw the guides |
| `--checks "<kind>: on, …"` | turn kinds of finding on or off, over the file |
| `--no-checks` | print no findings; errors still print |
| `-v`, `--version` | print the version |

`reladraw serve diagram.reladraw` opens a page for the diagram that redraws whenever the file changes and can edit and save it, `reladraw serve` with no file opens the playground on this machine, and `reladraw note` describes a change made to a served file; see [A page that follows its file](#a-page-that-follows-its-file).

`reladraw install-skill` installs the agent skill that came with this version of reladraw, for every project, by running `npx skills add` on it with `--copy`. `--claude` installs it in `~/.claude/skills`, `--agents` in `~/.agents/skills` (Codex and others), and both may be given; with neither, it asks, or, with no terminal to ask in, refuses and names them. For any other agent it prints the `skills` command to run.

The output is a standalone SVG: every picture is drawn into it as path data, never from a font or a linked file. A web page can draw a diagram in place with `<reladraw-diagram>`; see "In a web page" in the README.

### A page for looking at a diagram

```
reladraw render arch.reladraw --page
```

`--page` writes `arch.html`: one self-contained file, for opening in a browser, attaching or committing, that needs nothing running and fetches nothing. The page is in the diagram's own colors, so a dark diagram doesn't sit on a white page, and it is headed with `diagram title:`, or the file's name when there is none. Under the title it says which file it was drawn from and when, such as "drawn from arch.reladraw, 2026-11-05 14:32": the page is a snapshot of the file, and is behind it once the file is edited, until it is rendered again. Drag to pan, or press `g` to grab the diagram and pan it with the arrow keys or `h` `j` `k` `l` (Shift for bigger steps, `g` or Escape to let go); scroll, pinch or double-click to zoom; Fit shows the whole diagram and 100% returns it to its own scale. The zoom is always shown, with "Fit" beside it while the whole diagram is in view. There is a full-screen button. The Export menu saves the page itself, as it was written rather than at its current zoom; the `.reladraw` source it was drawn from; or the picture as an SVG or a PNG, as `render` would draw it; or copies the SVG. Each is named after the source file: `arch.html`, `arch.reladraw`, `arch.svg`, `arch.png`. In Chrome and Edge it asks where to save; other browsers put the file with their downloads. The findings are listed beside it, and clicking one lights up what its line drew. A box's or a line's name shows under the pointer.

**The Settings menu** holds the page's settings, each row a switch that says on or off. **Theme** opens a list of themes, and draws the diagram in the one picked, as `--theme` would, keeping the view and the selection; a page or text color the file states holds in every theme. It starts on "Diagram's theme", the one the file names (or dark), which follows the file when it is rendered again. A theme picked by name is the reader's: it holds on every reladraw page in that browser, whatever the file says, until "Diagram's theme" is picked again. **Side panel** shows or hides the panel beside the drawing, which then stays hidden whatever is selected. **Auto-hide panel** shows it only while something is selected or the findings are open, and the findings start folded. Both are remembered by the browser for every page. **Findings**, with their count, open or fold the findings in the panel. **Guides**, with their count, draws the [guides](#guides) as `--guides` does; it starts as the file or `--guides` says, and a change lasts for that page only. Save SVG, PNG and Copy SVG take the theme and the guides as shown.

**From the keyboard**, `m` reaches the bar: it is ringed, each control shows its letter, and a strip under it names where the keys are and which keys work there. `s` opens Settings, `x` opens Export, and `f` goes full screen. In a menu a row's letter does what the row does, and the menu stays open, so several can be changed in turn: in Settings, `t` theme, `p` side panel, `a` auto-hide, `f` findings and `g` guides; in Export, `p` this page, `r` the source, `s` SVG, `n` PNG and `c` Copy SVG. The arrow keys and Enter work too. In the theme list the arrows draw the diagram in each theme as they reach it, and Enter keeps the one reached. Backspace steps back one level at a time: from the theme list to Settings, from a menu to the bar, from the bar to the diagram, and then lets go of a grab, a lit finding and the selection in turn. Escape goes straight back to the plain diagram from anywhere: every menu closes, a theme tried and not kept is dropped, and a grab, a lit finding and the selection are all cleared. With the menus closed, `p` shows or hides the side panel and `f` goes full screen; `+` `-` `0` `1` zoom at every level.

**A click on a box or a line selects it**, and never follows a link. The selection is amber; what feeds it is green and what it feeds is red, the lines dashed and moving the way they run; the rest dims. A line runs from the end without an arrowhead when only one end has one, and otherwise from the end written first. The panel beside the drawing names the selection and lists its links, each with its badge, and the boxes it comes from and goes to; a link opens in a new tab, and a box selects it. One line out lights by default, and the panel's button lights everything upstream and downstream. Its description, if it has one, comes last ([Descriptions](#descriptions)). A box with links underlines its text under the pointer. A click on the background, Escape or Backspace clears the selection.

**Selecting from the keyboard**: `s` puts a letter on every box and line, and typing a letter selects that thing. Things in view get the one-letter labels; past 26, the rest take two letters. `/` starts a filter that narrows what gets a letter, live as it is typed: a plain word matches a box's or a line's text, `is:node`, `is:edge` and `is:container` match a kind, and `style:synced` matches what wears that style. Words combine, so `/is:edge rclone` letters only the lines whose text says rclone. Enter ends the filter and the letters pick again, or selects the match at once when there is only one. With something selected, `n` letters what is one line away (from a box, its lines and the boxes at their other ends; from a line, its two ends), `i` letters the boxes inside the selected box and the box it sits in, and `l` letters its links, which a letter opens in a new tab: on the side panel's rows when the panel is shown, and in a small list beside the selection when it is hidden. Backspace steps back a letter, then out of the filter, then out; Escape clears everything. A picked thing out of view is brought into it.

Keys: `+` and `-` zoom, `0` fits, `1` is actual size, `f` is full screen, `p` shows or hides the side panel, `s` and `/` select, `n` `i` `l` step from the selection, Escape clears the selection.

### A page that follows its file

```
reladraw serve arch.reladraw
```

`serve` opens the same page in the browser, served from this machine and tied to the file: whenever the file changes on disk, whoever changed it, the page draws it again, keeping the view, the theme and the selection. Under the title it says the page is live, and when the file was last read or changed. A file that stops drawing keeps the last picture that drew, with the error at the head of the findings, and draws again as soon as the file does.

The **Edit | View** switch beside the title (or `e`) shows the source beside the picture, colored as in the playground, and the picture redraws as you type. The source's **Help** menu holds the syntax reference and the **Cheatsheet** (or `?`), the language on one screen: a card per topic, each example colored as in the editor beside what it does, with a filter that keeps the rows holding every word typed. While the source is shown, the side panel stays out of the way unless something is selected, the source has an error, or the findings are opened from Settings. The divider between them can be dragged. **Save** (or ⌘S, Ctrl+S) writes the file, and nothing else does; a dot beside the file's name means there is text the file doesn't have. **Format** lays the source out as `reladraw format` would, with the nearest `.reladraw-format`.

If the file changes on disk while the editor holds unsaved text, the text stays, and a strip says the file changed, by whom when that is known, with **Load it** to replace the text with the file's and **Keep mine** to carry on. Saving over a change made since you started editing asks first.

**Versions** (or `o` from the bar) lists the file's versions since the server started, newest first: each one saved from the page, each change on disk, and each change an agent described with `reladraw note`, with its note. Picking one puts it in the editor as unsaved text, to save if you want it back. They are kept only while the server runs.

One server serves the folder it was started in, and only `.reladraw` files inside it, to this machine only. Serving another file from that folder opens its page on the server already running and returns at once. Ctrl-C stops the server, and an open page then says so; it follows the file again when a server is started in the same folder. `--no-open` prints the page's address instead of opening it.

**Export ▾ ▸ This page** saves the diagram as `reladraw render --page` would write it: a page to send, not one tied to the file.

```
reladraw serve
```

With no file, `serve` opens the playground, served from this machine: the source shown, with a **File** menu holding Examples…, Open… and Save…, and the format settings, with your text kept in the browser. Its first Save asks for a path inside the folder, such as `docs/flow.reladraw`, and asks before replacing a file already there. From then on the page is tied to that file, as if `serve` had been given it.

```
reladraw note arch.reladraw "moved the cache under the API"
```

`note` describes the change just made to a served file, for its Versions list, which shows it as an agent's. With no server serving the folder, it notes nothing, says so, and succeeds.

### Formatting

```
reladraw format diagram.reladraw other.reladraw
reladraw format --check diagram.reladraw
reladraw format - < diagram.reladraw
reladraw format --init
```

`format` lays each file out again in place. By default every statement is on one line, and neighboring statements with the same keyword line their clauses up in columns, each as wide as its longest clause plus two spaces; a blank line or a new keyword starts a new set of columns, and a comment line between them doesn't. A comment at the end of a line lines up with the others in its set. A statement written over several lines with a comment among them keeps its lines, with the indent tidied. Blank lines stay as written, and so do Windows line endings.

Inside a clause, spacing comes out as these pages write it, whatever was typed: one space after a key's colon and between words, none just inside a bracket, and a comma against the word before it, so `line:( corners:rounded , path:square )` becomes `line: (corners: rounded, path: square)`.

Only whitespace changes, and the order of clauses when `clause-order` asks: every word is copied as it was written, and the result is checked to draw exactly what the original did. A file that doesn't parse is reported and left alone, and the other files still run. `--check` changes nothing, prints each file that would change, and fails if there is one, for a pre-commit hook or CI. A shell expands `*.reladraw` into the files; folders aren't searched.

`-` in place of the files reads the diagram from standard input and prints it formatted, touching no file. That is how an editor formats a buffer, saved or not: Vim's `:%!reladraw format -`, or the command a format-on-save package runs. Its settings come from the nearest `.reladraw-format` to the current folder.

The settings are in the nearest `.reladraw-format`, in the file's folder or a folder above it; with none, the defaults. A project that puts one at its top keeps everyone's formatting the same. `reladraw format --init` writes one in the current folder with every setting at its default and a comment on what each value does, and refuses if one is there already. One setting a line, as in a diagram:

```
// keep each clause straight after the last
columns: off
clause-gap: 2
```

| setting | values, default first |
|---|---|
| `wrap-at` | `off`, or a number of characters: past it, a statement wraps onto as few lines as fit |
| `clause-per-line-at` | `off`, a number of characters, or `always`: past it, every clause gets its own line |
| `first-line` | `text` (keyword, name and texts), `name`: where a broken statement's first line ends |
| `clause-order` | `as-written`, or a list of kinds: `placement`, and keys by name, such as `style, placement, fill` |
| `columns` | `aligned`, `off` |
| `columns-shared-by` | `same-keyword-neighbors`, `neighbors`, `same-keyword` (across blank lines), `file` |
| `clause-gap` | a number of spaces, `2`; or `tab`, with `columns: off` only |
| `trailing-comments` | `shared-column`, `after-statement` |
| `comments-inside` | `keep-lines`, `move-above` (joined, comments above it), `refuse` (left alone, comment named) |
| `continued-lines-indent` | where a broken or kept statement's later lines start: `4` or another number, `tab`, `under-name`, `under-name + 2`, `under-text` (under the name when there's no text) |
| `blank-lines` | `as-written`, `exactly 2`, `at-most 3` |
| `edge-name-and-ends` | `one-column`, `own-columns` (name, each end and the arrow a column each) |

An unknown setting, one written twice, or a value it doesn't take is an error naming it.

**Breaking a long statement.** With both at a number, a statement up to `wrap-at` stays on one line, one up to `clause-per-line-at` wraps, and a longer one goes one clause to a line. Its length is measured as it would be printed, lined up with its neighbors, so a short statement pushed past the width by a long neighbor's columns breaks too; its first line still lines up with theirs. A statement that can't break, such as a node's name and text with nothing after them, is left as it is, even when its columns carry it past the width. A break falls only between clauses, never inside one or inside a bracket, so a clause longer than the width stands alone on its line, past it. A statement broken by hand is broken again by these rules, or joined when they leave it short enough; one kept on its lines for a comment among them is left as it is. A comment at the end of a broken statement follows its last line.

```
// wrap-at: 60
node  confirm  "Confirm"
    below accept (gap: tight)  left of accept (gap: wide)
    style: plain
```

**Ordering clauses.** `clause-order` lists the kinds of clause in the order they are written: `placement` for every relation, and a key by its name (`style`, `fill`, `via`). Kinds it leaves out follow, in the order written, and clauses of one kind keep theirs. A node's or edge's texts never move, since the language takes them only straight after the name; `text` in the list means a style's `text:` key. A clause never moves where moving it would change what the statement says.

## Attributes

Every attribute, and what takes one. A node's kind is what its body is: a box (`shape:`), a picture (`icon:`) or bare text (`shape: none`).

| attribute | box | picture | bare | line | says |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `style` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | the styles to wear, one or a list |
| `shape` | ✓ | | ✓ | | the outline |
| `icon` | | ✓ | | | the picture the node is drawn as |
| `badge` | ✓ | | | | a picture joined to the text |
| `cards` | ✓ | | | | a deck's cards, when they are only texts, front first |
| `fill`, `border` | ✓ | | | | colors |
| `corners` | ✓ | | | | `sharp` or `rounded`; only on a box's outline. A line's go in `line: (…)` |
| `text` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | in a style only; on a statement, the bracket after the text |
| `layout` | ✓ | | ✓ | | how the children are arranged |
| `gather-children` | ✓ | | ✓ | | where the children sit in spare room |
| `heading` | ✓ | | ✓ | | the child that is the title |
| `join-with` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | the thing this moves with |
| `description` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | text for the page's panel ([Descriptions](#descriptions)) |
| `padding` | ✓ | | ✓ | | room inside the edge |
| `padding-top`, `-right`, `-bottom`, `-left` | ✓ | | ✓ | | one side's room, over `padding` |
| `width`, `height`, `min-…`, `max-…` | ✓ | | ✓ | | a stated size |
| `overlap` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | | `allow`: an overlap is meant |
| `depth` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | drawn behind or in front of something |
| `url` | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | a destination |
| `from`, `to` | | | | ✓ | where the line leaves and arrives |
| `via` | | | | ✓ | the places it passes |
| `from-mark`, `to-mark` | | | | ✓ | the marks at its ends |
| `line` | | | | ✓ | its color, or everything about it in a bracket |

A point takes `style`, `fill` and `depth`; a region those, `opacity`, `border` and `padding`; a bundle `via`, `layout`, `order`, `line`, `from-mark` and `to-mark`.

**A word the table doesn't give the kind is an error.** A word that is an attribute nowhere is a misspelling, and the error lists what the kind takes. A word that is an attribute somewhere else is usually written on the wrong thing, so the error says where it belongs: `background:` on a node points at `fill:`, and `theme:` on one points at `diagram theme:`.

## What the language refuses

Deliberate omissions. What they protect is that the tool never *chooses* an arrangement: it computes the one you described.

- **Coordinates**, in any form. Every position is said relative to things the diagram contains, so it survives those things moving.
- **Guessing.** An axis nobody stated, an order nobody gave, a direction to separate two boxes, a way round a box. Each is refused or drawn as written and reported, never decided.
- **Avoiding.** A line goes where it is told and is reported where it crosses something. A box stays where it is placed and is reported where it overlaps.
- **Synonyms.** One spelling for each thing, and the others refused by name.
- **Silence.** An unknown key, an unknown icon, a word on the wrong kind of thing, a removed spelling: each is an error naming what to write instead.

Not on this list: saying more about where something goes. A statement that lets you be more precise is not a step toward auto-layout.

## Not built yet

Designed and absent from the code.

- **A line joining or leaving a bundle partway.**
- **Several marks at one end of a line**, such as a database's crow's feet.
- **Attributes, templates and functions**: definitions of your own that add placements, nodes and lines.

## Undecided

- `widths: match` on a hand-placed container, so "as wide as the widest of them" doesn't go stale.
- A text in a heading starts small, as bare text does, so a hand-built heading needs `(size: normal)` on its text. Whether it should start at a box's size is open.
- How a file sets its own unit.
- Spreading one side's line ends over the whole side.
- More layouts: `grid`, `star`, `circle`.
- Which side "faces" for two boxes placed diagonally. Today it is the side the line between their centers crosses; always across first is the other reading.

## Changelog

Pre-1.0, so the minor number is where a breaking change goes. Every removal is refused by name with the replacement quoted, rather than dropped in silence: an older file stops with an error saying what to write instead.

**0.29.0**

- **The playground and `serve`'s page check only when Check is pressed**, as the playground did before 0.28.0, with **Check as I type** in Settings to check on every redraw. While the source is shown, the findings appear in a band under the picture, with View all to open the side panel. See [Errors and findings](#errors-and-findings).
- **Edit is now an Edit | View switch** beside the title, and the side panel stays out of the way while the source is shown.
- **The View menu is now Settings**, opened by `s` from the bar.
- **The picture's controls float over it**: Check at its top left, and the zoom at its bottom right. The page's bar keeps Export, Settings and Full screen. Fit leaves room above and below for them.
- **The cheatsheet opens as a large window**, from the source's Help menu or `?`: a card per topic, examples in the editor's colors, and a filter. Help also links the syntax reference.
- The hosted playground's bar is one line: its name, with GitHub's mark linking to the repository.
- **In the playground, Examples, Open… and Save… are in a File menu** in the source's bar. A page tied to a file keeps its Save button.
- The source's buttons wrap onto a second row when the source is narrow, instead of running under the picture.

**0.28.0**

- **`reladraw serve` opens a page that follows its file.** The page redraws whenever the file changes on disk, edits it beside the picture, and writes it on Save or ⌘S. Unsaved text is never replaced by a change on disk without asking, and a Versions menu keeps the file's recent versions, saved from the page, changed on disk, or described by an agent with **`reladraw note`**. One server serves a folder. See [A page that follows its file](#a-page-that-follows-its-file).
- **`reladraw serve` with no file opens the playground** on this machine; its first Save names a file in the folder, and the page then follows that file.
- **The playground is the page.** It gains selection, the side panel, View and the keys. The Guides box and the theme picker are now in View, and the theme picked there no longer writes a `diagram theme:` line into the source. Check is gone: the findings are in the side panel and redone as you type. Examples, Open…, Save…, Format settings, the cheatsheet and the text kept in your browser are as they were.
- **The page's Save menu is now Export**, opened by `x` from the bar, so that Save can mean writing the file on a served page. On a page with an editor, Export's This page saves a snapshot, as `render --page` writes it.

**0.27.0**

- **The `--page` page selects from the keyboard.** `s` puts a letter on every box and line and a letter selects it; `/` filters what gets a letter by text, `is:node`, `is:edge`, `is:container` or `style:`; with something selected, `n` letters what is one line away, `i` what is inside it and the box it sits in, and `l` its links. See [A page for looking at a diagram](#a-page-for-looking-at-a-diagram).
- **The `--page` page has a View menu**, and its bar keeps only the zoom, Full screen, Save and View. The theme, the side panel, auto-hide and the findings moved into View, each a switch that says on or off, and View gained **Guides**, which draws the diagram's guides as `--guides` does. **`m` reaches the menus from the keyboard**: each control shows its letter, a strip names where the keys are, Backspace steps back one level and Escape goes straight back to the plain diagram, clearing the selection too. In the theme list the arrow keys try each theme on the diagram, and Enter keeps one. See [A page for looking at a diagram](#a-page-for-looking-at-a-diagram).

**0.26.1**

- `h` `j` `k` `l` now pan only while the diagram is grabbed with `g`, as the arrow keys do, on the `--page` page and in the playground. In 0.26.0 they panned without a grab.

**0.26.0**

- **The arrow keys pan a diagram**, on the `--page` page and in the playground. Press `g` to grab the diagram: a border and a hint show it is held, the arrows pan it a step at a time, and Shift makes the steps bigger. `g` again or Escape lets go, and the arrows go back to whatever else uses them. Clicking into a text field lets go too. `h` `j` `k` `l` pan the same way without a grab.
- **The `--page` page has a theme picker**, which draws the diagram in any theme without moving anything, and Save SVG and PNG save the theme shown. It starts on the diagram's own theme, which follows the file; a theme the reader picks holds on every page in that browser until they pick the diagram's theme again.
- **The `--page` page's side panel can be hidden**, with the Panel button or `p`, or set to Auto-hide, showing only while something is selected or the findings are open. A long description now fills the panel's height instead of scrolling in the top part of it. Closing the findings clears the highlight a finding lit.
- The agent skill now leaves out `diagram theme:` unless the user asks for a theme.

**0.25.1**

- The agent skill now says that a distance and a direction after `and` start a second placement, and how to name a point to use as a target. No change to what the tool accepts or draws.

**0.25.0**

- **A link can be declared once and used by name**: `url orders-docs "https://…" (name: "Docs", icon: "D")`, then `url: orders-docs`, so long addresses stay out of the statements that link to them. A declaration may list several links, declared names among them, and a `url:` mixes names and quoted addresses. See [Destinations](#destinations).

- **Marked text takes its style's size**: with `style dim  text: (size: small)`, `"Some Node / [dim]something[/dim]"` draws the second line small, and a line that is all small is spaced as one. Markup used to take only a style's color, and a style with only a size was refused as saying nothing about text. See [Markup](#markup).

- **`2 right of and 3 below a`** is accepted, the same as `2 right and 3 below a`. It used to be refused with a message that took `and` for the name of a box.

- **A distance and a direction after `and` or a comma start a second placement**: `node b  right of a and 2 above c top` puts `b` right of `a`, with its bottom 2 above `c`'s top. It used to take `2 above c top` as a point added to the targets, so `b` was placed right of the region covering `a` and that point, with no warning, and the second half looked ignored. To get that reading, name the point first: `point p  2 above c top-center`, then `node b  right of a and p`.

- **A box or a line can have a description**, shown in the panel when it is selected on a `--page` page, and as hover text in an SVG. It is written on the thing, `description: "Forwards each request by its path."`; at a distance, `description for orders and to-orders """…"""`; or named, `description replica """…"""`, and taken with `description: replica`. The text is a small part of Markdown: paragraphs, lists, bold, italic, code and links.

- **A line's text can rise a stated amount off its line, or part of the way clear.** `above edge` and its kin always moved a text all the way clear, which on a slanted line can be well away from it. `(1 above edge)` now raises it one unit from its spot on the line, still crossing the line if that is short of clear, and `(1/2 clear above edge)` moves it half the way. `(1 above edge)` used to be refused, pointing to `edge-gap:`.

**0.24.0**

- **`reladraw install-skill` installs for Claude Code, the `~/.agents` folder, or both, and asks which.** It used to pass everything on to `skills`, which, given no agent, put a copy in the folder of every agent it knows, more than fifty of them, and in the current project unless `-g` was written. It now always installs for every project, in the places `--claude` and `--agents` name; `-a` and the other `skills` options are refused with the `skills` command that does the same, and `-g` is still accepted.

**0.23.1**

- **`reladraw format` no longer fails on a comment between a placement and its bracket**, such as `right of a`, then `// why wide`, then `(gap: wide)` on lines of their own. It stopped with "Cannot read properties of undefined"; it now keeps the comment where it was. Reported in #22.
- **A comma in a name is refused by name.** `node a,b` has been refused since 0.19.0, but the message said "a text is quoted — write "b" rather than b"; it now says a name may not contain a comma, because a comma separates the items of a list. Reported in #23.

**0.23.0**

- **A box or a line can have several links**, each with a name and a badge: `url: "https://github.com/…" (name: "GitHub", icon: "GH")  "https://docs.example.com/…" (name: "Docs")`. In an SVG a click follows the first and the tooltip lists them all. See [Destinations](#destinations).
- **A click on the page selects a box or a line.** The page made with `render --page` lights what feeds it in green and what it feeds in red, and a panel beside the drawing lists its links and the boxes at either end. A click no longer follows a link on the page; the panel does. See [A page for looking at a diagram](#a-page-for-looking-at-a-diagram).
- **A line with no text can have a link.** It used to be refused as too thin to click; an unseen wider copy of the line now takes the click.
- **A letter icon**: `icon gh  letters: "GH"  fill: #24292f  text: white` is a few letters in a circle, usable anywhere an icon is. See [Your own icons](#your-own-icons).
- **The page can save its own source, and itself.** A page made with `render --page` now carries the `.reladraw` file it was drawn from, so whoever is handed the page can get the source back. Its Export menu is now a Save menu: This page, .reladraw source, SVG, PNG and Copy SVG, and in Chrome and Edge each save asks where the file goes. Under its title the page says which file it was drawn from and when, so you can tell whether it is behind the file.
- **The agent skill keeps throwaway diagrams out of your project.** A diagram drawn only to show you something now goes in a folder outside the project, such as `~/.cache/reladraw/`, and a project's own diagram gets its page there too. While fixing findings it runs `reladraw check`, so no stray SVG is left beside the source.

**0.22.1**

- **`reladraw format` keeps to `wrap-at` once the columns are lined up.** A statement's length used to be measured on its own, before it was lined up with its neighbors, so a short one like `node  api  "API"  layout: column` stayed on one line and was then padded out by a long neighbor's name to nearly twice the width. It is now measured as printed and breaks like any other long statement; `clause-per-line-at` is measured the same way.
- **Output sent to another program is no longer cut off.** `reladraw format -` and `reladraw render -o -` stopped after the first 64 KB when their output went into a pipe rather than a file, and still reported success, so an editor formatting a large diagram could replace it with a shortened copy. All of it now comes through.
- **The agent skill puts a link on the thing it belongs to.** Asked to add links, an agent would add a new text node for each one; the skill now says to give the existing node or line a `url:`. When a diagram's things have real web addresses, such as a pull request's files, it offers to link them rather than doing it unasked.

**0.22.0**

- **`reladraw install-skill`** installs the agent skill that came with your reladraw, so it teaches what your copy accepts rather than what the main branch does. It hands the work to `skills`, passing on `-g`, `-a` and the rest. The npm package now carries the skill.
- **The agent skill opens each diagram it draws as a page in the default browser**, with `reladraw render --page` as the last step of every drawing rather than only when asked to show it. It doesn't open one when there is no display, or when the user has said not to.
- **The page says when it is showing the whole diagram**: its zoom reads "Fit · 62%" while fitted, and just the number once you zoom or pan. The Actual size button is now 100%, which is what it always did. Save SVG and Save PNG are under an Export button, which can also copy the SVG.
- **The playground pans and zooms as the page does**: − and +, Fit, 100%, the wheel, a pinch, a drag, a double-click, and the keys + - 0 1, with the zoom shown between − and +. Its one Actual size button, whose label named the view you would go to rather than the one you were in, is gone. The view stays where you left it as you type. Copy SVG, Save SVG and Save PNG are now under one Export button, so the row of controls fits.

**0.21.0**

- **A diagram can have a title**: `diagram  title: "How a login reaches the database"`. The SVG carries it as its own title, which a browser shows on the tab. See [The diagram](#the-diagram).
- **`reladraw render --page`** writes a page for looking at a diagram: one self-contained HTML file in the diagram's colors, headed with its title, that pans, zooms, goes full screen, saves the SVG or a PNG, lists the findings and lights up what each one is about. See [A page for looking at a diagram](#a-page-for-looking-at-a-diagram).
- **A border can be thicker or thinner**: `border: (color: #d2904e, thickness: thick)`, mirroring the line's bracket. A thick border is drawn inside the box, and the box grows to keep its padding, so it may move what is placed beside it. See [A border's bracket](#a-borders-bracket).
- **A box can be lined up with something inside a box placed against it.** `node a "Node A"  even with b.1` with `node b "Node B" right of a` used to be refused, "nothing anchors the diagram", because `right of a` also centered B on A. That centering now gives way, as it already did to a placement written on B itself, and B goes where B.1 is level with A.

**0.20.0**

- **`stays above`, `stays below`, `stays left of` and `stays right of`** keep a child placed in its box's corner clear of the other children: `node laptop.mark  icon: laptop  inside laptop top-right  stays above laptop.photos`. The laptop stays in the corner, and the box makes room. See [Against its own parent](#against-its-own-parent).
- **Breaking: a corner and a sibling saying the same axis are refused.** `node c.j "j"  inside c top-right  right of c.k` used to be centered between the two, neither in the corner nor beside `c.k`, straddling the box's edge. The error offers `right of c.k  inside c top` to sit beside `c.k`, and `stays right of c.k` to keep the corner. The same goes for `inside c top-right  above c.k` up and down.
- **A new finding, `node-overflow`**: a child placed in its box's corner or against its side that the box has no room for there, such as `node drive.mark  icon: disk  inside drive top-right` on a box one line tall. It used to run out of the box with nothing said.
- **A child in its box's corner that covers one of the box's other children is reported** as `node-overlap`, with the `stays` that would keep it clear. Being placed `inside` a box used to excuse it from covering anything in that box, not only the box.
- **A child beside a sibling and against its parent's top stays inside the parent.** `node c.j "j"  right of c.k  inside c top` used to be drawn wholly outside `c`, with nothing reported. Being against the parent's top only measures its height from the finished box; across, the box holds it like any other child.
- **Breaking: a hex color without its `#` is refused.** `fill: 444444` used to be passed to the viewer as is, which drew nothing. The error says to write `#444444`.
- **The playground saves a PNG** with Save PNG, at twice the picture's size, in the fonts the page shows it in. Download is now Save SVG beside it.

**0.19.1**

- **A copy that states its own `step-out:` or `turn:` keeps it.** Lines between the same two sides of the same two boxes fan into lanes, and each used to be drawn as the first one's shape shifted over, so a `step-out:` or `turn:` written on any later line was ignored. A line naming either is now drawn as written and leaves the fan, and so does a line named in its side's `right-edge-order:` list. Where that puts two lines on one run, it is reported as `edge-overlap`. Prompted by #19.
- **Errors and findings name a named line by its name**, as written: `line e2 b.1 -- b.2 runs on line e1 b.1 -- b.2`. Two lines between the same boxes used to read identically.

**0.19.0**

- **`reladraw format`** lays a file out again: each statement on one line, neighboring statements with the same keyword lined up in columns, comments kept beside what they are about. No word is respelled, and the result is checked to draw what the original did. `--check` fails on a file that would change, and `.reladraw-format` holds a project's settings; `reladraw format --init` writes one with every setting explained. `reladraw format -` reads standard input and prints the result, for editors. A long statement can wrap past a width (`wrap-at`) or go one clause to a line (`clause-per-line-at`), and `clause-order` puts placements and keys in a chosen order. The playground has a Format button (Shift+Alt+F, undone with Ctrl+Z) and a panel for its settings, which can copy them as a `.reladraw-format`. Spacing inside a clause is evened out too: `gap:tight` becomes `gap: tight`, `( gap: tight )` becomes `(gap: tight)`. Prompted by #14, where a long statement was hard to read in a plain editor.
- **A comma may touch the next word or stand apart from both.** `(corners: rounded,path: square)` used to be refused with "`corners` has no value", and `(at: start , above edge)` was refused in a text's bracket; both now read as `rounded, path:` and `start, above` do.
- Breaking, and missing from this list when 0.19.0 shipped: a name may no longer contain `,`. `node a,b` used to declare a node called `a,b`; the comma now ends the name, so the file is refused. Added after the fact, from #23.
- **The playground opens and saves `.reladraw` files**, with Open… and Save… above the source. Save suggests the name of the file last opened or saved; Chrome and Edge ask where to put it, other browsers save it with the downloads. Opening a file over edits that haven't been saved to one asks first.
- **The playground's error message can be copied**, with a Copy button beside it or by selecting it. Only the underlined line number jumps to the line now; a click anywhere on the message used to, which took a selection away.
- **The playground no longer fails on some diagrams with 0.18.0's shapes**, which stopped with "insidePolygon is not defined". The command line was unaffected.
- **The agent skill checks it matches the installed tool.** It compares its own version with `reladraw --version` and tells the user which of the two to update.

**0.18.0**

- **More shapes, for flowcharts and the rest** (#18): `diamond`, `pill`, `parallelogram`, `hexagon`, `trapezoid`, `triangle` and `cylinder`, named for how they look, and the flowchart standard's shapes that have no geometric name as `flow-` and what they mean, from `flow-subprocess` and `flow-delay` to `flow-collate`. A shape's settings go in a bracket after its name: `shape: parallelogram (slant: 2, lean: left)`, `shape: cylinder (lying)`, `shape: document (fold: 1.5)`.
- **A shape grows to hold its text at its middle**, and a stated `width:` and `height:` stretch it. Its sides are the stretches of outline round its points, so `from: right` leaves a diamond from its right point.
- **A circle given a `width:` and a `height:` that differ is an ellipse.** It used to stay round and say nothing about the height.

**0.17.1**

- **`reladraw --version`**, or `-v`, prints the version.
- **The playground waits for a pause in typing** before it redraws a diagram that is slow to draw, so the keystrokes aren't held up behind it. A quick one still redraws on every keystroke. Suggested in #6.

**0.17.0**

The redesign. The tool no longer decides anything the file doesn't say: a gap is exact, nothing moves a box to make room, lines are straight unless told and go only where they are told, and anything that may not read as meant is drawn as written and reported as a finding. Almost every diagram written for 0.16.0 needs changes; the table below gives each old spelling and what to write instead.

Breaking, in how things are drawn:

- **Gaps are exact.** A gap used to be a minimum that other things could widen. Now it is the distance, and nothing widens it.
- **The gap words changed size**, and a number is in the file's unit, not pixels. `tight`, `normal` and `wide` were 24, 56 and 110 pixels; they are now 2, 4 and 8 units of 12 pixels (24, 48 and 96). `gap: 12` was 12 pixels and is now 144; write `12px`, or `1`.
- **Nothing pushes overlapping boxes apart.** Two boxes placed on one spot are drawn there and reported as `node-overlap`.
- **Identical placements no longer make a list.** Three nodes `right of hub` used to stack into a column; now they sit on one spot, reported. Put them in a container with `layout: column`.
- **A container's unplaced children no longer stack.** A container needs `layout: column` or `row`, or exactly one unplaced child with the rest placed against it.
- **A child placed against its parent's side no longer grows the parent.** It is placed against the finished box.
- **Opposite placements no longer push their targets apart.** `right of a  left of b` centers the box in the space already there.
- **A line's text no longer makes room for itself**, and no longer slides off other texts. It sits at the middle of its line unless placed, and overlaps are reported.
- **The patch behind a line's text takes the color beneath it**, such as a container's fill, where it was always the page's color and showed as a dark box on a tint. `fill:` in the text's bracket sets it, `none` for none.
- **A deck is a container, `layout: deck`, and its cards are its children**, the front one first, so each card has a name and the deck is the whole stack. `node drive "Drive 1"  deck: "Drive 2" "Drive 3"` is written `node drive ""  layout: deck  cards: "Drive 1" "Drive 2" "Drive 3"`, and a front card that holds things is written out with every card as a child. `deck:` is refused, quoting the new form.
- **Lines are straight by default**, `path: straight`. They were curved. `default edge  line: (path: curved)` keeps the old look.
- **Lines no longer find their way round boxes.** A line goes straight, or square or curved along a route read off its own two boxes, and through anything in between, which is reported. `via:` says where it goes. Lines no longer take lanes from each other; copies of one line still fan.
- **A line with no side named meets the side facing the other box.** It used to aim at the other box's center; `from: center` does that.
- **A line out of a side flush against another box, or between two touching boxes, is drawn and reported**, where it used to be refused.
- **A container's title is centered along its top.** It was at the top left; `(inside top, align: left)` keeps that.
- **A container inside a container is a shade lighter** (darker on a light theme) than the one it sits in. It used to take the same fill, so only a faint border told them apart. `fill:` sets it as before.
- **A badge is part of the label.** The text and its picture are placed as one unit, so a badged box with nothing else in it draws as a leaf, and `badge:` is allowed on `default leaf` and `default node`.
- **A text's `size:` number and a line's `thickness:` number are multiples of normal.** `size: 22` used to be 22 pixels, and is now 22 times normal, with no error; write `size: 22px`. `thickness: 3` likewise; write `3px`.
- **The command takes a verb**: `reladraw render diagram.reladraw`. The bare form is refused.

Breaking, in spelling:

| 0.16.0 | now |
|---|---|
| `level with a`, `top level with a` | `even with a`, `top even with a` |
| `gap: wide` on a node | in the placement's bracket: `right of a (gap: wide)`, or `8 right of a` |
| `contents: (widths: match, align: center)` | `layout: column (widths: match)`; `gather-children: center` for where the group sits |
| `align:` in a layout's bracket | `align-children:` in the bracket, or `gather-children:` on the box |
| `below of a`, `left a` | `below a`, `left of a` |
| `edge a -> b  between c and d` | `via: between c and d` |
| `edge a -> b  between c and d vertically` | `via: between c and d`, or `via: through r horizontal` through a named region |
| `edge a -> b  below c` | `via: c bottom` |
| `edge a -> b  above c`, `left of c`, `right of c` | `via: c top`, `via: c left`, `via: c right` |
| `"Title" (at: top-left)` on a node | `(inside top, align: left)` |
| `(at: center)` on a container's text | `(center)` |
| `(at: …)` on a leaf's text | nothing; a leaf's text is centered, or `(inside top)` and the other sides |
| `reladraw diagram.reladraw` | `reladraw render diagram.reladraw` |
| `size: 22` | `size: 22px` |
| `thickness: 3` | `thickness: 3px` |
| `gap: 12` | `gap: 12px`, or `1` |
| `from:` or `to:` in a style, which did nothing | on each edge: `edge a -> b  from: right  to: left` |
| `node drive "Drive 1"  deck: "Drive 2" "Drive 3"` | `node drive ""  layout: deck  cards: "Drive 1" "Drive 2" "Drive 3"`; a front card holding things is written as a child, `node drive.1 "Drive 1"`, and so is every card |

New:

- **Points and regions.** `between a and b`, `down from a and left from b`, `up from c and even with d top`, `2 below c bottom`, named with `point` and `region`, usable anywhere a position is.
- **Waypoints.** `via:` lists the places a line passes: a side, a point, a box, a region, a leg of another line. Legs can be named.
- **Square and curved routes** read off a line's own two boxes, with `turn:`, `step-out:` and `curve:`.
- **Line ends at points**: `from: bottom-center`, `to: left 3/4 down`, `from: center`, an end on another line, `straight down`, and a line's place among others on a side, `to: top, right of z`.
- **A line's end even with another thing**: `from: right, even with cat1` leaves the right side level with `cat1`, and heads straight out. Lines out of a tall box can each run level with a box beside it without working out fractions of its height. A height that misses the side is refused.
- **Named lines** and points on them: `req start`, `req end`, `req at 1/3`.
- **A line between points and regions**: `edge a -> b` where `a` and `b` are named points, regions or boxes, in any mix, guide lines included. A point end is exactly on the point; a region end is like a box's.
- **Bundles**, parallel, collapsed or fanned, with a stated `order:`; a bundle between two boxes routed as a line is, `bundle logs  web -> ops  from: bottom  to: top  line: (path: square)`, its lines side by side the whole way; `edge each child of a -> b`, and lines to several ends, `edge a -> b, c, d`.
- **Texts on lines placed** along the line, on a leg, on its longest level piece, by a box, or beside the line, and turned with `reads:`; the patch behind one takes `fill:` and `padding:`.
- **A line from a box back to itself**, as a loop round a side: `edge job -> job  from: left  to: right  via: job top  line: (path: square)`.
- **Placing across containers**: a child may be placed against a box outside its container, `node host.bin  top even with cat0`, and a container whose children are placed that way, with none unplaced, goes where they put it.
- **A direction beside a pin**: `below trx  top even with cat0  bottom even with nice` keeps `below` for lining up under `trx` and checking it holds, and takes how far down from the pins.
- **The order of the lines on a side, listed on the box**: `node a  right-edge-order: ae, ad, ac`. A line's own `below ae` works on `from:` as on `to:`, and several form one chain whatever order they are written in.
- **`straight` from a spot on its side**: `from: right 1/4 down  straight right` leaves from that spot rather than the side's middle.
- **A curved line runs straight under its arrowhead**, so it goes into the head along its axis instead of bending out of its side.
